Mr Speaker took the Chair at 2 p.m.
Prayers.

items.speaker: Hon SIMON POWER
items.text: Next week it is the
Government’s intention to make furthe r progress on the Marine and Coastal Area
(Takutai Moana) Bill.

items.speaker: Hon TREVOR MALLARD
items.text: Can I seek from the Acting
Leader of the House an undertaking that there is a continuanc e of the previous
undertaking not to take that bill under urgency.

items.speaker: Hon SIMON POWER
items.text: Correct.
Customs Training Programme—Graduates

items.speaker: Hon MAURICE WILLIAMSON
items.text: I draw to the House’s
attention that in the gallery today we have a stunning group of fine New Zealanders who
are graduating from the customs training programme and becoming customs officers.
Earthquake, Christchurch—Government Support for People Affected
1. Hon ANNETTE KING (Deputy Leader—Labour) to the Prime Minister: Is he
satisfied that all systems set up pursuant to commitments he has given to assist residents
following the Christchurch earthquake are appropriate and working?
Hon BILL ENGLISH (Deputy Prime Minister) on behalf of the Prime Minister:
Generally yes, but due to severe damage in the eastern suburbs some households may
well be without power, water, and sewerage for some time yet. However, I want to
assure people that everythi ng that can be done is bein g done to restore essential
infrastructure.

items.speaker: Hon Annette King
items.text: Will he ask the Minister of Finance to issue a direction under
section 12 of the Earthquake Commission Act requiring prompt and direct payment for
rebuilding in Christchurch, in light of comments by the master plumbers’ chairman,
Mark Whitehead, and builder Nick Rogers, who said today that they are refusing to
carry out rebuilding work for the Earthquake Commission because they do not get paid,
and they are now requiring distressed homeowners to pay cash up front before any work
is done?

items.speaker: Hon BILL ENGLISH
items.text: I do not think that the Earthquake Commission would need a
direction to ensure that it does as much as it can do to expedite the rebuilding process. I
understand the pressure particularly on contractors who were expecting the rebuild from
the first earthquake to be well under way now. That has been delayed by maybe a month
or two. But we will work with the commission to ensure it does it as fast as it can.

items.speaker: Hon Annette King
items.text: In light of that answer, will th e Prime Minister ask the Minister
of Finance to take urgent steps to ensure  contractors and subcontractors who are owed
thousands of dollars by the Earthquake Commission for emergency work done after the
September quake are paid, given that in orde r to avoid their businesses failing, with the
loss of hundreds of jobs, some businesses have already taken out loans to stay afloat?

items.speaker: Hon BILL ENGLISH
items.text: Certainly, if there are contractors who have not been paid,
and who should have been paid according to normal credit terms, then the Earthquake
17118 Questions for Oral Answer 10 Mar 2011
Commission should get on and do that. But I think the signif icant shorter-term problem
concerning the construction indus try in Christchurch was its expectation that it would
be gearing up quite rapidly now, and that has been delayed by the second earthquake.
All the parties involved, though, now have a gr eat deal more experience in how to get
this work under way faster, and I hope it will be under way faster than last time round.

items.speaker: Hon Annette King
items.text: Does he agree with Mayor Bob Parker that landlords who are
hiking up rents on houses and business premises in Christchurch are “looting by another
name”, and has he considered taking action similar to that of the Federal Government of
the United States following Hurricane Katrina, when it limited the increase in rents, etc.
to no more than 10 percent to prevent greedy landlords from profiting from other
people’s misery?

items.speaker: Hon BILL ENGLISH
items.text: We would share the mayor’s c oncern if there is significant
profiteering. The Government will be liste ning to the advice of the Minister for
Canterbury Earthquake Recovery, who is on the ground and also shares those concerns.

items.speaker: Hon Annette King
items.text: Who is collating and acting on information about vulnerable
residents—for example, elderly people who are living alone, people who are bedridden,
and those with disabilities—when some ha ve been visited several times by various
agencies, including M āori wardens, the police, the army, social agencies, etc., and
others have not been visited at all, and how can the Government ensure that these
people get the assistance they need?

items.speaker: Hon BILL ENGLISH
items.text: As the member has pointed out, a number of agencies regard
it as their obligation to contact vulnerable people who simply do not have the capacity
to deal with the difficult circumstances they find themselves in. There is quite a bit of
work going on to try to coordinate those efforts, to ensure that there is complete
coverage and no one is left out.

items.speaker: Hon Annette King
items.text: I raise a point of order, Mr Speaker. I really appreciate that
answer, but would the Minister be able to tell us by whom —that is the issue. Who is
collating and acting on this information? That is the core of the question.

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: What I will do is to allow the member to repeat her question, but do
keep it succinct.

items.speaker: Hon Annette King
items.text: Who is collating and acting on the information about vulnerable
citizens in Christchurch, some of whom ha ve been visited by many agencies and some
have not been visited; who is ensuring that they get the services they need?

items.speaker: Hon BILL ENGLISH
items.text: I would not want to give the member an exact answer about
that specific task. It is quite likely that the Ministry of Social  Development is the
primary Government agency for delivery of the contact by telephone calls, the social
assistance with the Earthquake Commissi on assessors—social workers going around
with the assessors—and setting up the ne ighbourhood offices that give more people
easier access to the support. But I will check to see whether the ministry is performing
that particular task.

items.speaker: Hon Steve Chadwick
items.text: What procedures will be fo llowed when determining which
heritage buildings damaged by the earthquake will be demolished?

items.speaker: Hon BILL ENGLISH
items.text: I cannot answer that question in detail, because it is the
subject of discussion between the civil defen ce controller, the Minister for Canterbury
Earthquake Recovery, and the Christchurch Ci ty Council. But clearl y there needs to be
a transparent and predictable process for dealing with that issue.

items.speaker: Hon Steve Chadwick
items.text: Does he agree with the co mments of the Minister for
Canterbury Earthquake Recovery on the preservation of heritage buildings: “There is a
need to move fairly quickly”, and “if I had my way they’d be down tomorrow.”?

items.speaker: Hon BILL ENGLISH
items.text: The Minister has expressed a view that a number of older
buildings that, after the firs t earthquake, were regarded as heritage buildings worth
10 Mar 2011 Questions for Oral Answer 17119
preserving have now collapsed and killed peopl e. He has expressed the view that some
of those buildings should be dealt with, be cause they are dangerous. We would expect
that regardless of whether they are heritage  buildings, if they are a danger to public
safety they should be dealt with shortly.
Economy—Reserve Bank Forecasts, 10 March 2011
2. DAVID BENNETT (National—Hamilton East)  to the Minister of Finance :
What do this morning’s Reserve Bank economic forecasts show?

items.speaker: Hon BILL ENGLISH
items.text: The forecasts show that both
consumer spending and business investment in creased only modestly in the second half
of 2010. There were recently so me signs of an upturn but the earthquake has had a
significant impact. The immediate impact will be to cut GDP by about 0.6 percent in the
March quarter, and the Reserve Bank believes that growth this year will be relatively
weak. The earthquake impact comes on top of an economy that was already a bit weaker
than expected before Christmas.

items.speaker: David Bennett
items.text: What is the outlook for interest rates and exchange rates over the
next few years?

items.speaker: Hon BILL ENGLISH
items.text: Although the Reserve Bank is fo recasting growth to peak at
over 4 percent in 2013 and unemployment to reach below 5 percent, it believes that the
interest rate cycle will  be relatively subdued. Inflation is  expected to be stable, and the
picture on interest rates is si milar. Although the current low o fficial cash rate will not
last indefinitely, the bank projects that 90- day rates will lift gradua lly to 4.6 percent by
2014, which is a low peak compared with the last cycle, where the official cash rate
reached almost double that figure.

items.speaker: David Bennett
items.text: What discussions took place between the Government and the
Reserve Bank prior to today’s official cash rate announcement?

items.speaker: Hon BILL ENGLISH
items.text: More discussion took place than  usual. About 2 weeks ago,
just after the quake, the Reserve Bank contacted us and suggested that in the presence of
a national emergency policy makers might best be mutually informed of the likely crisis
response. We agreed and we briefed the bank on the emergency measures that the
Government was taking and how it was likely to impact on the 2011 Budget. The bank,
in turn, described its own economic forecasts , its thoughts on the appropriate stance for
monetary policy, and the availa bility of cash and banking se rvices in Christchurch. At
all times the official cash rate decision re mained with the governor; I was not entirely
sure until this morning what the decision would be.

items.speaker: David Bennett
items.text: What are the implications of toda y’s forecasts for the rest of the
Government’s programme?

items.speaker: Hon BILL ENGLISH
items.text: It is good to see that the pr ojections of the Reserve Bank
include increases in household savings. According to the bank, New Zealanders will
continue to increase their savings rate. Th e bank expects that the Government will be
back to financial surplu s around 2014-15. This projecti on fits in with our own
intentions.
Official Cash Rate—Reduction
3. Hon DAVID CUNLIFFE (Labour—New Lynn) to the Minister of Finance: By
what amount has the Reserve Bank lowered the official cash rate today, and what reason
has the bank given for this action?

items.speaker: Hon BILL ENGLISH
items.text: As the member will know, the
governor has reduced the official  cash rate by 50 basis poi nts to 2.5 percent. It noted
that the Christchurch earthquake had cau sed considerable di sruption. Although it is
difficult to know how large or long lasting th is will be, the bank has said that economic
activity will be negatively affected. Secondly, the Reserve Bank noted, as I have
17120 Questions for Oral Answer 10 Mar 2011
previously in the House, that before th e earthquake the growth was weaker than
expected through the second half of 2010, because households had been careful with
their money and the agricultural  sector has been paying o ff its debt. The Reserve Bank
noted that the signs that the economy was picking up in early 2011 have been more than
offset by the earthquake.

items.speaker: Hon David Cunliffe
items.text: By how much did the Reserve Bank revise downwards its
estimate of economic growth in the last quarter of 2010 in today’s Monetary Policy
Statement?

items.speaker: Hon BILL ENGLISH
items.text: I cannot give the member an exact answer, but I am sure it
did revise it down. I think if we go back we will find that it has revised down its
forecasts for two or three quarters of this year, as well.

items.speaker: Hon David Cunliffe
items.text: Given that the bank has re vised down its pre-earthquake
forecast for the last quarter of last year, a nd confirmed that the economy was either flat
or in recession for the last two quarters of la st year, can the Minister say how much his
tax cuts stimulated the economy, given the bank’s comments that “Even before the
earthquake, GDP growth was much weaker than expected”?

items.speaker: Hon BILL ENGLISH
items.text: It is always hard to judge wh at might have happened if we
had not put up the tax package.  I think it is impo rtant to remember, though, that the tax
package was broadly fiscally neutral. It was not expected to stimulate the economy,
because whatever people were getting through income tax cuts they were paying back to
the Government through higher GST or higher tax on property.

items.speaker: Hon David Cunliffe
items.text: Have households been net savers  or dissavers in the last 2
years according to Reserve Bank data released today?

items.speaker: Hon BILL ENGLISH
items.text: I think the data will show that—to use the member’s term—
the rate of dissaving has slowed. In 2007 New Zealand households were spending
something like $1.11 for every dollar they earned. The Reserve Bank forecasts show
that we will have positive savi ngs rates over the next 12 or 18 months for the first time
in 20 years. That is good for the economy.

items.speaker: Hon David Cunliffe
items.text: Given that the Reserve Bank has confirmed today that it
estimates households will not actually start positive saving until 2013, and have
continued to increase their borrowings sinc e the Minister took office, how can he
possibly blame the deepening national recession on household saving?

items.speaker: Hon BILL ENGLISH
items.text: Well, I disagree with the member’s idea of a deepening
national recession. The fact is that the us ual way in which the New Zealand economy
recovers is for people to go b ack to the shops, go back to the housing market, and start
spending on the back of easier credit. That is simply not happening this time, because
banks are not going to lend more money to people to drive up house prices and to
encourage retailing. So people are saving, and they are getting on top of their debt. That
means a flatter economy in the short term but a stronger one in the long term.

items.speaker: Hon Sir Roger Douglas
items.text: Will the Minister explain to the Prime Minister that his
instructions to the Governor of the Re serve Bank on interest  rates only create
uncertainty in the minds of investors, particularly overseas investors, thereby killing off
a good deal of investment that might otherwise have taken place?

items.speaker: Hon BILL ENGLISH
items.text: There were no instructions to the Reserve Bank governor.
As he said this morning, he made the decisi on about interest rate s on his view of the
economy.
Fuel Prices, Increase—Effect on Economy
4. GARETH HUGHES (Green)  to the Minister of Finance : What will be the
impact of the recent fuel price rise on the New Zealand economy, including impacts on
GDP, consumer spending, and the current account?
10 Mar 2011 Questions for Oral Answer 17121

items.speaker: Hon BILL ENGLISH
items.text: The impact on each of those amounts
will be adverse, but it is too early to sa y by how much. The spike in oil prices has
happened fairly quickly, with prices trending up since September last year. The rise in
prices at the pump has been boosted by the recent weakness of the New Zealand dollar,
although that weakness in the New Zealand dollar is generally beneficial to the
economy. What happens from here depends on how long the lift in international prices
is sustained.

items.speaker: Gareth Hughes
items.text: Does he agree with analysts at Morgan Stanley, who say that sharp
increases in global oil prices pose the biggest threat to th e global economy and that the
last five major recessions followed oil price shocks?

items.speaker: Hon BILL ENGLISH
items.text: I think we are all c oncerned about the impact of a sharp rise
in oil prices, in terms of both the pressure  it could put on house holds and the way it
takes more resources from our economy to keep petrol and diesel running. However, we
are resilient. The latest spike is not yet as big a spike as the one experienced in 2008.
We have plenty to do to get this economy in better order, but we cannot actually
influence the oil prices.

items.speaker: Craig Foss
items.text: What impact has the general lift in commodity prices had on New
Zealand’s income and economy?

items.speaker: Hon BILL ENGLISH
items.text: We need to keep in mind that  part of the general lift in
commodity prices is record high prices fo r the commodities we sell, as well as higher
prices for the ones we buy, such as oil. The net impact is measured by terms of trade.
Overall, our terms of trade have lifted 25 percent in the past decade. New Zealand has
been a net beneficiary from th e significant increase in comm odity prices, including the
price of oil.

items.speaker: Gareth Hughes
items.text: Does he expect—as many comme ntators expect—that the next
decade will see continuing oil price spikes?

items.speaker: Hon BILL ENGLISH
items.text: It is possible. That is why, if we are to expect continued
instability in oil prices, we need a resilient economy that is able to adapt quickly both in
a straight economic sense and in terms of how people live their lives.

items.speaker: Gareth Hughes
items.text: Why does New Zealand not have a strategy to reduce our current
vulnerability to higher oil prices, as many other countries do?

items.speaker: Hon BILL ENGLISH
items.text: People are pretty sensible. Wh en they see prices going up,
they start thinking about whether they want  to continue with their energy-intensive
business or lifestyle. As it happens, over th e years New Zealand, as I understand it, has
become less energy-intensive in its producti on, which is a trend that will probably
continue if oil prices keep going up.

items.speaker: Gareth Hughes
items.text: How is spending $10 billion on new motorways reducing our
vulnerability to higher oil prices?

items.speaker: Hon BILL ENGLISH
items.text: Spending on the motorways creates a more efficient traffic
system whereby commuters get better value ou t of what they invest in their cars, bus
fares, and petrol. We are keen to make sure we finish the current roading infrastructure
investment because, despite the earthquake, it is important for New Zealand’s long-term
productivity and standard of living.

items.speaker: Gareth Hughes
items.text: For Kiwis who are struggling at the pump at the moment, how will
the $10 billion the Government is spending on motorways help Kiwis who start walking
or cycling and who flock to the buses and trains, as large numbers did in 2008 during
the last oil shock?

items.speaker: Hon BILL ENGLISH
items.text: It will help in two ways. It means that when they catch the
bus it will actually spend more of its time trav elling than sitting at the traffic lights.
Buses are the most common form of public transport, and they need efficient roads to be
effective. They cannot be run on railway tracks. It is the same with cars.
17122 Questions for Oral Answer 10 Mar 2011

items.speaker: Gareth Hughes
items.text: Will the Minister finally support an inquiry into how New Zealand
can best protect its economy from high oil prices?

items.speaker: Hon BILL ENGLISH
items.text: Probably not. When we talk about strategies to deal with
high oil prices, we see that the fact is that the best strategy is for people to see the price
signals and change their behaviour accordi ngly. The Greens understand that strategy
because it is the theory and practice behind the emissions trading system, which is
precisely about sending a price signal to pe ople, although in that case it is about carbon
usage.
Question No. 5 to Minister

items.speaker: Hon DAVID PARKER
items.text: I raise a point of order,  Mr Speaker. Given that
neither the Minister for Economic Developm ent nor the Acting Minister for Economic
Development is in the Chamber, I seek l eave to carry over my question to the next
sitting day.

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: Leave is sought for the question to be carried over to the next sitting
day. Is there is any objection to that? There is objection.
Economic Development, Acting Minister—Duration of Appointment
5. Hon DAVID PARKER (Labour)  to the Acting Minister for Economic

items.speaker: Development
items.text: Has he been advised by the Prime Mi nister whether his appointment as
Acting Minister for Economic Development is temporary or expected to carry on to the
election?
Hon SIMON POWER (Acting Leader of the House)  on behalf of the Acting

items.speaker: Minister for Economic Development
items.text: No. The advice the Actin g Minister received
from the Prime Minister is the same as what  he has stated public ly—namely, that these
changes have been made for the foreseeable future and will be kept under review as the
recovery progresses.

items.speaker: Hon David Parker
items.text: Given that his appointment is, as he has just said, for the
foreseeable future, can he please tell the H ouse what new plans he has to halt the slide
in the New Zealand economy?

items.speaker: Hon SIMON POWER
items.text: I can do no better than borrow a phrase from history used by
the Hon John Tamihere in response to a sim ilar type of question, and that answer was
“Heaps!”.

items.speaker: Hon David Parker
items.text: Is the Minister aware that there are already low levels of
confidence in the economy, and does he th ink it was wise, then, for members of his
Government to add to New Zealanders’ feelings of insecurity by softening up the public
for possible cuts to Working for Families and student loans?

items.speaker: Hon SIMON POWER
items.text: In respect of the second part of the question, I do not
believe that is what the Minister did, or what the Government has done, in any case.

items.speaker: Hon David Parker
items.text: Given those very low levels  of confidence, why is the
Government continuing to speculate on effec tive increases in taxes for middle-income
New Zealanders via cuts to Working for Families and student loans?

items.speaker: Hon SIMON POWER
items.text: The member opposite should not assume any of those things
and should wait and see what the Government has in store.

items.speaker: Hon David Parker
items.text: Why can the Minister not see th at more responsible leadership
is needed to ensure that the wheels of the economy turn rather than  fall off, and when
will he bring forward some new ideas to get the economy running?

items.speaker: Hon SIMON POWER
items.text: In respect of the first part of the question, responsible
leadership in these areas is well and truly entrenched and under way.
10 Mar 2011 Questions for Oral Answer 17123
Public Transport, Wellington—Rail Network Improvements
6. KATRINA SHANKS (National)  to the Minister of Transport : What action is
the Government taking to improve Wellington’s train network?

items.speaker: Hon STEVEN JOYCE
items.text: Today I announced a further
funding package from the Government that will bring Wellington’s metro rail back up
to a high and reliable standard for commuters. The Government is committing a further
$88 million for the upgrade of the remaining signalling and power supplies in
Wellington. In addition, the Government will also co-fund the Greater Wellington
Regional Council’s $80 million refurbishmen t of the 30-year-old Ganz Mavag units
with the help of the New Zealand Transpor t Agency. This funding comes on top of the
existing $383 million upgrade, which includes the new Matangi trains.

items.speaker: Katrina Shanks
items.text: What other changes have been announced today as part of the
package?

items.speaker: Hon STEVEN JOYCE
items.text: The Greater Wellington Region al Council has agreed to
share the cost of, and respons ibilities for, delivering thes e and future improvements to
Wellington’s rail system. The New Zealand Transport Agency will now fund rail on the
same basis as it funds other forms of public transport, including a move to a 50 percent
funding rate over 10 years, but also funding the capital improvements. The council will
pay a realistic track access charge to Kiwi Rail, with a subsidy from the New Zealand
Transport Agency that reflects the fair cost  of maintaining the track and other assets.
The Wellington rail network has been a cons iderable and ongoing source of frustration
for many commuters and it took the previous  Government a huge amount of time to get
around to doing anything about it. This package, coupled with the previous investments,
will transform the service into a modern, reliable public transport option for
Wellingtonians.

items.speaker: Chris Hipkins
items.text: Why is the Government not fundi ng the full cost of the Wellington
rail upgrade, which will mean that Wellingtonians will face increased rates to fund the
rest of it, and why should they  not feel like they are getting the rough  end of the deal,
given that he is spending 15 times what  he has allocated for Wellington rail on his
“Holiday Highway” north of Auckland?

items.speaker: Hon STEVEN JOYCE
items.text: I realise that Mr Hipkins is  one of the Labour Party people
who thinks that Government money is cos tless, but, actually, it is not; it comes from
taxpayers. This is a very good partnershi p between taxpayers; the Greater Wellington
Regional Council; KiwiRail, which is contri buting some assets; and the New Zealand
Transport Agency, which is contributing tran sport subsidies. It is a very good package
and I am sure that the member could endorse it because it wi ll be very good for
Wellingtonians, including members of his own electorate.

items.speaker: Kris Faafoi
items.text: Will the Minister reassure Wellington rail commuters that they will not
face fare increases until the service has actually improved; if not, why not?

items.speaker: Hon STEVEN JOYCE
items.text: If the member had done his research he would know that
the fares for Wellington rail are set by the Greater Wellington Regional Council, not by
the Government. That happens to be the reality of it. It is im portant to note, as we have
said previously, that many years of mism anagement of the Wellington rail network—
including a good number of years by the previo us Government before it got its act into
gear and started making some form of inve stment—has meant that there has to be a
catch-up, which has to be met in a fair wa y between all the stakeholders, including
passengers, ratepayers, and taxpayers.

items.speaker: Hon Sir Roger Douglas
items.text: Has the Minister seen the comments of Dr Roderick Deane
in a recent speech that the rail network will be valued at $14.5 billion by 2015, yet
17124 Questions for Oral Answer 10 Mar 2011
KiwiRail will not generate any surpluses over the next 5 years, and does he agree that
pouring money into projects that do not yield any return is a sure path to fiscal crisis?

items.speaker: Hon STEVEN JOYCE
items.text: There is a whole range of an swers and I am struggling to
pick one. The point that I would make to Dr Deane is that one has a sunk asset that one
has to decide whether one is going—

items.speaker: Hon Trevor Mallard
items.text: I raise a point of order, Mr Speaker. I just wonder whether
instead of leaning over, the member could—

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: No, I will not have that.

items.speaker: Hon STEVEN JOYCE
items.text: One would think the member for Hutt South would have
some interest—

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: We will not have any of that. The House will come to order.

items.speaker: Hon STEVEN JOYCE
items.text: The important thing, whic h perhaps Dr Deane does not
realise, is that passenger transport in  both Wellington and Auckland—and, in fact,
around the world—have never made profits. They provide congestion benefits to
motorists, which is why public transport subsidies are in place. In regards to his other
assertions about the rail networ k generally, I do have concerns about the value of that
asset. The Government certainly has concer ns and we think the previous Government
overpaid hugely to return that  asset to the public fold. We are making the best of a bad
situation and seeking to get the best possible return we can from that asset.
Pike River Mine Tragedy—Government Funding for Recovery of Victims
7. Hon DAMIEN O’CONNOR (Labour) to the Prime Minister: Can he assure the
families of those killed in the Pike River mine  disaster that Government funding will be
available for the recovery of bodies, given the mine is now in the receivers’ hands?
Hon BILL ENGLISH (Deputy Prime Minister) on behalf of the Prime Minister:
As the Government has said many times, the key issue in deciding whether the recovery
of the bodies could take place is the safety  and stability of the mine. Money has not
been an issue.
Hon Damien O’Connor: How can the grieving families of the 29 Pike River miners
trapped in the mine be reassured that ever y effort is being made to recover their
remains, when receiver John Fisk has stated  that “the body recovery operation is the
responsibility of the police and that operation stopped some time ago.”, and when the
receiver has now announced the possible sale of the whole mine?

items.speaker: Hon BILL ENGLISH
items.text: The recovery operation by the police came to an end simply
because it appeared to be making no progress in the face of the difficulties of stabilising
the mine and making it safe to go in there. Authorities such as th e police maintain the
same interest in the recovery of the bodies, regardless of who owns the mine.
Hon Damien O’Connor : Can the Prime Minister then assure the families that any
new owner of the mine will also have a legal and moral obligation to pay for the
recovery of the remains of their loved ones who are still trapped in the mine?

items.speaker: Hon BILL ENGLISH
items.text: The member is raising some complicated issues, I think, to
do with conferring an obligati on on an owner in the face of the stability and safety
problems in the mine. That is a matter that no doubt we could get some advice on, but I
would simply restate the case: money has not been an issue. There has been significant
money spent there in order to try to get some safety and stability in the mine.
Unfortunately, that has not occurred, but the au thorities still maintain the same interest
in the cause of death and the recovery of those bodies.
Hon Damien O’Connor : Does the Prim
e Minister’s statement “I gave a
commitment to the families at Pike River th at I would do everything I could to get their
men out and I stand by that” mean that he will guarantee to fund th e recovery of their

remains, or is that statement about as reliable as the one that stated he would not
increase GST?

items.speaker: Hon BILL ENGLISH
items.text: I will not dignify that comment on the very real commitment
that all people have shown towards the recovery of those bodies. If the member wants to
make a political circus out of it, that is up to him. Those bodies are still there. The
Crown has taken every step it possibly can. The hurdle is the safety and stability of the
mine—not the receivers, not the new owners. There is no other obstacle but the safety
and stability of the mine. If the efforts made  by the police to try to secure the mine had
been successful, of course we would be in  there recovering those bodies. No one has

viable way to do it.
Earthquake, Christchurch—Replacement Toilets
8. COLIN KING (National—Kaik ōura) to the Minister of Civil Defence : Is the
Government satisfied with the provision of replacement toilets for earthquake-affected
Christchurch residents?

items.speaker: Hon JOHN CARTER
items.text: The answer is yes; 88 percent
of Christchurch City now has water, and it is expected that by the end of this weekend
95 to 96 percent of households will have water.  As for the other 4 percent, because it is
difficult to ascertain the situation, we are asking those people who do not have water by
the end of the weekend to ring 941 8999 to te ll the Christchurch City Council. We want
those homes to get water on and the toilets to then be flushed so that we can ascertain
whether the sewerage system is working. We ask them to check in their backyards and
in their streets to see whether there are any difficulties, and if difficulties occur, we ask
people to ring 941 8999 to tell the council. About 60 percent of homes, as we
understand at the moment, have usable toilets. The problem we  have is that there is so
much siltation in the pipes that we need to carry on ascertaining the damage, and many
of those pipes will have to be jet-blasted so  that we can know what is there. In the
meantime, 40,131 temporary toilets, both Port aloo toilets and chem ical toilets, have
been sourced. Some have yet to arrive, but civil defence is getting them into
Christchurch and out to affected people as quickly as possible. We are using military
personnel to deliver the temporary toilets. I can tell members that I was speaking with a
controller just before I came down to the House, and the toilets are being checked
regularly to make sure we are delivering them as widely as we can.

items.speaker: Colin King
items.text: Is the Government concerned about the possible outbreak of disease, in
the light of sanitary cond itions and the need for nei ghbourhoods to share Portaloo
toilets?

items.speaker: Hon JOHN CARTER
items.text: Yes, we are, of course. Co mmunicable disease risks from
gastroenteritis are being monitored, planned for, and managed. So far no unusual spikes
have been seen. In media conferences and advisories, civil defe nce and Ministry of
Health officials continue to remind residents to boil drinking water, regardless of where
it comes from. They should also boil water that is being used to clean wounds. Advice
includes reminders to wash hands or use hand sanitisers. Free hand sanitisers are
available from water-tanker sites.

Earthquake, Christchurch—Continuity of Early Childhood Education and
Schooling
10. ALLAN PEACHEY (National—T āmaki) to the Minister of Education: What
provisions have been made to ensure c ontinuity of early ch ildhood education and
schooling in the Christchurch region since the 22 February earthquake?

items.speaker: Hon ANNE TOLLEY
items.text: I am pleased to inform the House
that, as of this morning, 80 schools and 165 early childhood education centres have
opened. In addition, at least another 30 schools and 45 early childhood centres have said
that they are planning to open either tomo rrow or on Monday. This means that by the
beginning of next week approximately 40,00 0 students will be back at school and
continuing their education. Around the country a number of Christchurch children have
enrolled in other schools. To give school s certainty we are e ffectively double-funding
these students by funding them in their new sc hool and in their original Christchurch
school. This and other measures are expected to cost around $20 million.

items.speaker: Allan Peachey
items.text: What provision has been made fo r the students of those schools that
are so severely damaged that they will not be able to open this term?

items.speaker: Hon ANNE TOLLEY
items.text: Schools in Christchurch are being extremely flexible and are
looking at very innovative solutions to ensure continuity of schooling. In some cases we
are looking to share school si tes. For example, next week  Shirley Boys High School
will share the Papanui High School site, with Pap anui High School using the classrooms
in the morning, and Shirley Boys High School using them in the afternoon. In other
cases we are putting relocat able classrooms on to school  playgrounds. Where schools
can open but do have severe infrastructure  issues, we are working on a number of
solutions. For example, the Defence Force is  working to develop temporary sewerage
systems, and we are bringing water on to school  sites. The Farmy Army has also helped
to clear the results of liquefaction at 10 school sites.

items.text: What reports has she had of the in itial response to the earthquake in

items.speaker: Hon ANNE TOLLEY

their earthquake drills, and the children we re very well rehearsed. We have had no

teachers, and other school staff for their support for pupils. I have had reports that

Earthquake, Christchurch—Search and Rescue Progress
12. KANWALJIT SINGH BAKSHI (National)  to the Minister of Internal

items.speaker: Affairs
items.text: What reports has he received on the pr ogress of urban search and rescue and
firefighter teams working in Christchurch following the 22 February earthquake?

items.speaker: Hon NATHAN GUY
items.text: I have received daily reports
and updates since the earthquake. The Ne w Zealand Fire Service attended 3,919
incidents between 22 February and 7 March. This figure includes 155 rescues and just
under 2,000 property-related incidents. Curren tly five urban search and rescue task
forces are deployed from Ne w Zealand and overseas, whic h include 295 highly trained
personnel. More than 500 build ings have now been cleared and the focus is moving
from large buildings in the centre to smaller structures further out.

items.speaker: Kanwaljit Singh Bakshi
items.text: Has the Minister received any report about an increased
number of volunteers wanting to join th e Fire Service since the Christchurch
earthquake?

items.speaker: Hon NATHAN GUY
items.text: Yes, I have received some very positive reports of New
Zealanders wanting to help out by becoming fi refighters. I am told that the number of
website inquiries to the Fire Service ha s tripled since the ea rthquake, and that
applications have increased from an average of five a day to more than 15 a day since
the earthquake. This is very encouraging news because the Fire Service relies heavily on
both volunteer and professional firefighters to help New Zealanders in times of need.
Procedure

items.speaker: Hon SIMON POWER
items.text: I seek leave for the
introduction and passing of the Canterbury Earthquake Commemoration Day Bill prior
to 6 p.m. today.

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: Leave is sought. Is there any objection to that course of action being
followed? There is none.
First Reading

items.speaker: Hon KATE WILKINSON
items.text: I move, That the Canterbury
Earthquake Commemoration Day Bill be now read a first time . I thank the House for
supporting the passage of this bill through all its stages today.
The bill provides for 18 March 2011 to be a day of commemoration in those parts of
Canterbury—that is, in northern and central  Canterbury—that obs erve Christchurch
Show Day as Canterbury Anniversary Day, in order to commemorate the devastating
consequences of the Canterbury earthquake on 22 February 2011 at 12.51 p.m. Just over
2 weeks have passed since Christchurch wa s shattered by its second major earthquake.
This bill has been introduced to allow for the people of Canterbury to take a day to
come together as a community, and as a regi on, to grieve together and mark an event
that has so deeply affected each and every one of us. We are sti ll in the response stage
10 Mar 2011 Canterbury Earthquake Commemoration Day Bill 17131
of the earthquake. There is an enormous amou nt of work left to do, and that will be
ongoing for years, but next Friday we want to take the time to provide an opportunity
for all of Canterbury to mourn. It will also be a chance to celebrate the lives of those
who have been lost. There is no denying that the wounds are still open for everyone to
see. Next Friday’s memorial service will not bring an end to the grieving process, but I
hope it will help Canterbury at the beginning of this long road ahead.
This bill provides for next Friday to be observed as a public holiday known as
Canterbury Earthquake Commemoration Day. Canterbury Earthquake Commemoration
Day is to be treated, in those part of Cant erbury that observe Christchurch Show Day as
Canterbury Anniversary Day, as  a one-off public holiday for the purposes of the
Holidays Act 2003, and as a day to which s ection 65C(1) of the Education Act 1989
applies, which requires schools to be closed.
The provisions of the Holidays Act 2003 governing observance and payment for
public holidays will apply to Canterbury Earthquake Commemoration Day as follows:
employees are entitled to be paid if Canterbury Earthquake Commemoration Day, 18
March 2011, would have been a normal working day for them. If employees do not
work on Canterbury Earthquake Commemoration Da y, they are entitled to be paid what
they would have earned had they worked on the day; if employ ees work on the day,
they should be paid at least time and a half  for the time they actually work on that day.
They are also entitled to an  alternative holiday if the day would have been a normal
working day for them.
I am aware that this will place some unexp ected costs on some businesses in the
region, and of course this was taken into c onsideration when the Government discussed
creating a one-off public holiday for the regi on. However, there was no getting away
from the fact that this eart hquake is the greatest tragedy ev er to strike the Canterbury
region. Most people in Canterbury will want to attend the memorial service, but without
a public holiday it would be much more difficult for many of them to do so. It is
important that all of Canterbury is able to ta ke a day to mark this tragedy, and we hope
that businesses in the region will support th is public holiday. Many businesses are not
able to operate right now, and the Government is providing support to them and to
thousands of employees.
The welfare of the people of Canterbury is what matters most at this time. I expect
that tens of thousands of people will want  to attend the memorial service, and I
encourage everyone who can get to Hagley Pa rk to do so. The Government considers
that to mark a very significant event, it is appropriate to have a public holiday for the
people of northern and central Canterbury. I commend this bill to the House.

items.speaker: Hon ANNETTE KING
items.text: The Labour Opposition will
be supporting the Canterbury Earthquake Commemoration Day Bill. We are determined
to work alongside the Government and the community to make sure that Christchurch is
a better place for everybody, including our ch ildren. One way we can do that is to
ensure that this day of commemoration is able to take place.
I am one of those who have been to Christchurch over the last 2 weeks, on two
occasions, and I have seen firsthand the deva station and the impact on the lives of so
many people; not only people who live in Cant erbury but also family and friends right
around New Zealand. I do not think I have ever  seen such devasta tion in one of our
cities or towns in New Zealand. We have had many disasters over many years, but I do
not think I have seen, in my lifetime, such devastation.
Yesterday I went to Lyttelton, and unless one has been there one will not believe that
almost that entire town has fallen down. It will take a lot of hard work to rebuild it, as it
will in many parts of the city of Christchurch. As we have said on a number of
occasions over the last 2 weeks, we feel for the people of Canterbury and we want to be
17132 Canterbury Earthquake Commemoration Day Bill 10 Mar 2011
part of the rebuild of that area as fast as we  can. We want to ensure that they have the
opportunity to work, live, and play in a most wonderful part of New Zealand. As a
former South Islander who trained there as  a school dental nurse, I have a lot of
affection for that city.
We believe it is appropriate to set aside a day for the people of Christchurch to
mourn for the staggering loss of life. I woul d, however, have to say that it would feel
better if we knew the names of all those who had passed away; if we knew whom we
were commemorating. There is a feeling of em ptiness that there are only so many who
at this stage are identified as having passed away. I understand the terrible work that has
to be done in identification, and I say to the Minister of Police that the work the police
have been doing is absolutely amazing. They will do it thoroughly, and they will ensure
people know that the remains returned to them are those of their loved ones. I
understand that, but I feel that a commemoration should really be about commemorating
those who have lost their lives, and we will be  in a situation where this day is held but
we will not know whom they all are.
It makes one wonder whether at some stage there needs to be some other
commemoration. Perhaps a year after this event,  when we have been able to identify
everybody and when people’s minds have been  put at rest, we will be able to
commemorate this terrible disaster together as a country. We also believe that by having
a day to commemorate, people will be able to  stop and reflect on wh at they would like
to see happen in their own region and their own city. That is important.
One of the things that was said to me ove r and over again when I was in Canterbury
is that Cantabrians must have a say in what happens to their city. They must have a say
in how it is developed, designed, and built. I th ink that is a strong message we must all
take on board when we think of the people of Christchurch. If we th ink about it as if it
were our own back yard, it would be wrong and we would feel a ggrieved if somebody
said to us: “This is how you are going to have your own domain, and we’re going to
make the decision for you.” So I think there is a clear message to us.
Those of us who would like to see a re build happen quickly should stop, take a
breath, and think about how we can ensure that there will be a rebuild of that city that
has the buy-in of many, many of those people. We know that the economic cost to us as
a country, along with the social cost, is huge if we do not get the rebuild of that city
right. So when we commemorate and when pe ople are thinking about it, I urge us to
consider the views of Cantabrians and what they would like to see happen.
There is no need for us to panic in terms of the re-establishment of the city. We, with
the people of Canter bury, have an opportun ity to ensure we bu ild a city of the 21 st
century, the like of which we do not have in this country. We will look back in 100
years’ time and say that out of that devastation and rubble  has grown a city that is
providing economic and social susten ance to many, many people over many
generations.
Labour members support this bill, and we wi ll ensure we are represented at that
memorial service. I know that the Lead er of the Opposition, alongside the Prime
Minister, will be speaking on that day, maki ng it a parliamentary occasion. I think that
is important, because it is not a Government occasion. We have been talking across this
House about how we stand toge ther. It is important, I th ink, that the commemoration
service represents political parties across th e political divide, so people can see we are
together in commemorating with them the lo ss of so many lives. We stand here to
support this bill and commend it to the House.

items.speaker: Hon JUDITH COLLINS
items.text: It is truly humbling to speak on the
Canterbury Earthquake Commem oration Day Bill. I have just returned from
Christchurch for the third time since the earthquake of 22 February.
10 Mar 2011 Canterbury Earthquake Commemoration Day Bill 17133
I will just take a moment to deal with an issue raised by the member who has just
resumed her seat, the Hon Annette King, in re lation to the memorial day and the fact
that it is a shame we do not yet have all the names released of those who have lost their
lives. I am fully aware that we may never ha ve all the names of those who have lost
their lives, such has been the devastation that has been wreaked on some individuals. As
that member has acknowledged, the police are doing their very best to get absolute
accuracy in relation to the rema ins of those deceased, so that  they are returned to the
correct families.
We should not underestimate the dreadful jo b the disaster victim identification
teams—DVI teams—have had to endure. I visi ted them at their work. I can say only
that it is quite clearly the Lord’s work, because I am not sure that too many other people
would do it. They do the most amazing job. When the bushfires in Victoria went
through and killed over 200 people, it took over 6 weeks before any victims could be
returned to their families. Our team was returning them after a few days. It is a stunning
effort from some fantastic people. I take th is opportunity to thank all of the people who
have been part of that team—all of the people from around the world and from around
New Zealand who have been part of it.
This memorial day is about those who have died, but it is also about the many
survivors in Canterbury who have to live with the fact that they have lost loved ones or
friends, and about those who have had their businesses an d everything el se destroyed
around them. All they have left is their ow n lives. When we look for anything positive
we can take from that terrible day of 22 February, it would have to be the absolute value
of human life. Those who are still alive, even  those who have lost limbs, have had their
backs or necks broken, and have the most dreadfu l injuries, still have life. They cling to
life and they wish to live it as fully as they can.
I know there will also be people who think th is service will make things harder for
many businesses, because it is another paid day off. But I say that we should think about
those people who have continued to go to work through all of this. Think about our
police, our corrections officer s, our nurses, our doctors, and our council workers, who
have been collecting the rubbish off the str eets to try to do what they can. Think about
the people who have been trying to reconnect  sewers. Think about the people who have
been doing all the plumbing and the electricians—the people who have been working all
the way through. This is a day that we owe to Canterbury.
I recently read a comment in an Australian magazine about this quake. It said, for all
Australians, today they are Kiwis. I say to this House, for all New Zealanders, today we
are Cantabrians.

items.speaker: Hon TREVOR MALLARD
items.text: I want to join with members
in the tone of this discussion. I was not going to start this way, but I will acknowledge
the work of the police and the teams they ha ve developed. It must be pushing 15 years
since I spent a number of night s out with the police in my city. On one of those early
occasions I was with a team that was i nvolved in cleaning up after a road accident
where someone had hit a power pole and the remains were spread over 50 to 70 metres
down a road. The police officers were usi ng tweezers to pick up body parts. The police
and others in Christchurch—our other he roes—are doing that on a scale 200 times
bigger, and that is an enormous effort. It is almost like under every boulder, brick, and
stone they lift there is a possibility of finding part of a loved one. It must be so hard, yet
in a way I am sure for many of them it is rewarding.
I have had discussions with people from my area who have been involved in the
work, just as there are people in Christch urch from every area in New Zealand. Police
from my area have been in Christchurch a nd have come back. In a funny way it must
also be enormously rewarding work to be part  of a tea m that is now doing the best that
17134 Canterbury Earthquake Commemoration Day Bill 10 Mar 2011
can be done in returning as much of the remains of the loved ones to the families as they
can for appropriate burial or other disposal. It is hard work, and we thank them for it.
Perhaps a related question is that of whether there can be some informal arrangement
or direction from the commissioner that the police and others who have already worked
in Canterbury and who are now back home can be taken off active duty at least for the
period of the memorial service, so that th ey can be part of the commemoration. I think
that would be a good thing, and it should probably apply to the fire service and other
personnel as well.
I say to the Minister of Labour—again, I thi nk it will be a matter of the discretion of
individual employers—that th ere are now tens of thousa nds of Cantabrians who are
outside Canterbury. Many of them are worki ng for nationwide employers or are outside
their normal place of work in the Canterbury province. I wonder whether the Minister—
and she might like to report at a later stage—could encourage employers to treat those
Cantabrians who are now outsi de Canterbury as if they were in Canterbury for the
purposes of the commemoration. Because of the television aspect to the
commemoration, I think a lot of us will want to  feel a part of it, and it would be good
for those who were in Christchurch or who w ould normally be there to be allowed to be
part of it. I think gentle encouragement coul d be given for that to  occur. I do not think
we need an amendment to the legislation, bu t if we can get some leadership from the
Government on arrangements for the police and paid firefighters at least, then that
would be a good way of progressing.
As well as acknowledging those people, an en ormous number of public servants in
Wellington as well as in Canter bury have been burning the candle at both ends in order
to best respond to this terribl e event. We need to acknowledge them and thank them. In
fact, I tell the Minister of Police that the police with whom I have had a discussion have
had some arrangement where they have been down in Christchurch for a week. I think
they went down on the ferry late in the afte rnoon of the earthquake and stayed there for
a week. There was not one occasion when th ey had their normal 9-hour break between
shifts. They were always working for at least 16 hours a day, and often longer. There
will be some issues that flow from that.
Before I get back to that point, I acknowledge Anne Tolley and the work she and her
team have done. Through informal links—and occasionally some tears on Lambton
Quay—I have caught up with what has been going on within the Ministry of Education
and its team. I acknowledge her leadership and the work that Karen Sewell and those
people have done in order to make the best pos sible arrangements at this stage. It is an
enormous job. It could have gone much wors e. There will be enormous challenges to
come, and I am sure that at the appropriat e time we will give Anne Tolley some hurry-
up to make sure the good work continues. She has taken some leadership there, and part
of it has involved some additional funding, so me double funding, in order to make sure
that arrangements are appropriately in place for schools.
I want to go back to the Mi nister of Police and ask that she too looks at the effect on
police district budgets as a result of the earthquake work arrangements. Because of
briefings on the Rugby World C up, I know that this year will  be enormously tight for
the police. As far as leave is concerned, th ere are large blocks of time when the police
will not be able to take leave, and theref ore there will be an accumulation of leave. I
understand that the Minister of Police has al ready approved the paying out of time in
lieu for police who have been in Christchurch  where that is appropriate. I say to the
Minister of Police that I think we should not pressure some of the police who have been
in that situation to take payment of time in lieu unless they choose to. As a result of
working for a week, some of them have eff ectively accrued about 3 weeks’ leave. If
some of that is paid out, that is good. But I just want to make sure that the funding
10 Mar 2011 Canterbury Earthquake Commemoration Day Bill 17135
arrangements are in place in the same way that the Minister of Education has arranged it
for schools, so that policing is not reduced as a result of the exercise.
I know it is a matter that  will take some work ing through and it is not as urgent as it
is in respect of education, but it is a very real question. Having b een involved in some
negotiations in the past as the Associate Minister of Finance—if I take off my shoes and
do some counting on my fingers—I think about a week’s policing from the Hutt was the
loss of an officer for about 6 months. That ge ts to be quite a serious drop in a relatively
small community, so we need to work though it.
I will finish on what might be a slightly discordant note and say, as our leader and
deputy leader have indicated, that because the Government has made this decision, and
because of our determination to stand beside  the Government in these matters, we will
be supportive of it. I just want to toss in my  personal view now, which is that it might
have been better to wait a little while until  we had an understanding of who died, or at
least as good an understanding as we will ever get. I know of a relatively close friend
and acquaintance who has died, but whose na me has not been released. I do not know
whether others are on that list. I think that a ll of New Zealand is thinking about that at
the moment. At Pike River we knew who the 29 were. But we do not know in this case,
and my view is that it might have been better to leave it a bit longer until we do.
But what is clear out of all of this is that at some stage in the future we have to work
out what a proper memorial is. I want to think in grander ways than the physical for that
sort of memorial. Thank you.

items.speaker: KEITH LOCKE
items.text: The Green Party will be fully supporting the Canterbury
Earthquake Commemoration Day Bill. Since the horrific 22 February earthquake New
Zealand has been mourning those who tragically  were killed in that earthquake, and our
hearts are very much with their families at th is very difficult time. In a myriad of ways,
New Zealanders have been extending their support to those who survived and those
whose lives have been very badly affected. This support takes many different forms,
more than I think I have seen in New Zealand in as long as  I can remember. It includes
everything, from the official response by civil defence—and I see that John Carter is
with us today, and civil defence has done a tremendous job—right through to the very
grassroots things such as people having a little sausage sizzle in their street in suburban
Auckland and sending the money as their cont ribution to those who have suffered. We
particularly feel for those at the front line, the medics and search and rescue people who
are uncovering such horrible sights that none of us would ever want to experience. I pay
tribute to people from all levels of soci ety, on behalf of the Green Party, for the
wonderful response across New Zealand.
It is appropriate that we have a more fo rmal opportunity as a nation to mourn what
has happened and those who have died, a nd the ceremony on 18 Ma rch will provide
that, but I must admit that when I first he ard the Prime Minister’s  announcement of the
date, my instinctual reaction was that it was too soon. Many of the bodies of the victims
have not yet been identified and returned to their families. As of today, only 65 of the
166 bodies have been identified, and the families of most of the deceased have not had
the opportunity to properly grieve with their loved ones. However, I think this memorial
service will help those families, including the families of the overseas citizens who died,
mainly in the CTV building. They will all get to see that the whole of the New Zealand
community is behind them and with them in their grief.
I hope that the ceremony, to be held a week tomorrow, is more down-to-earth than
many of the ceremonies that we as parliament arians are involved in. An image in my
mind is of a whole lot of dignitaries in suits , ties, and for mal regalia, and that clashes
with another image that is in my mind fr om the time I spent goi ng door-to-door in the
suburb of Aranui, of people who have not been able to wash their clothes for more than
17136 Canterbury Earthquake Commemoration Day Bill 10 Mar 2011
2 weeks, whose toilet is a bucket, and who will find it quite difficult to travel over the
cracked and bumpy roads to even get to the Hagley Park event. I certainly hope that
they do get there.
It is unfortunate that ha ving a public ceremony so soon and declaring a public
holiday has provoked quite a bit of angst a nd controversy amongst the good citizens of
Christchurch, which can be seen in the blogs and in the comments on the TV3 website
at the moment, for example. All the point s made by people in Christchurch on those
websites and blogs are relevant , even if they do clash a bit with each other. Some
business owners who are already on their kn ees have complained about missing a day’s
work, or the cost to them of a paid holiday. Others have replied in the comments section
in blogs that the additional cost to busin ess should not override the importance of
collectively remembering the tragedy and huge loss of life. Both sides have a point, and
we should welcome such public discussion not only now but also in terms of the future
of Christchurch.
I think that whether it be on such matters  as the memorial day, which heritage
buildings to reconstruct, or whether to continue with the Rugby World Cup at AMI
Stadium in Christchurch, we should be open to  that discussion. It worried me a little bit
to read today that reports on the state of AMI Stadium would be shared with the
International Rugby Board before the people of Christchurch were told. It seems to me
that there needs to be a good public disc ussion about whether the Rugby World Cup
games should go ahead at that Christchurch  stadium, weighing up all the pluses and
minuses, and there are a lot on either side. I am worried that there might be a fait
accompli announcement by the Government, the International Rugby Board, or the
Rugby Union. I hope I am wrong about that, becaus e although it is likely that there will
be a reduction in the financial return if th e games are held in Christchurch and there
would certainly be many other difficulties with holding the games there, this needs to be
balanced against whether the games would be  an important morale boost for the people
of Christchurch.
Although this memorial service is dedicate d to remembering those who died in the
earthquake, it will inevitably be to some de gree an opportunity to express our feelings
towards all those in Christchurch who have  suffered, and who are still suffering, as a
result of the earthquake. Just about everyone living in the ea stern half of Christchurch
has suffered some degree of trauma, and their nightmare has not  ended. Nerves are
frayed from not knowing just how big the next aftershock will be, how much extra
damage it might cause, and whether they will be hurt. Then there is the sadness at the
loss of precious items in the big quake, wo rries about when homes will be repaired—if
they can be—and where the money might come from. Add to that the daily grind for the
many who are living without water and sewerage for the indefinite future. The memorial
day will be an opportunity to remember those whose lives were lost, but we will also be
thinking of those whose lives are now badl y damaged and who are living in their own
version of hell.
However, the story of Christchurch is also the story of great resilience, of community
spirit and togetherness. When going door-to-door in Aranui offering food and support, I
came across a front lawn with a substantia l fireplace and a pile  of wood on it. The
neighbours had been cooking food together. The next-door neighbour commented that it
should not take a disaster to bring people together. But together they now are, and this
story is repeated across the affected suburbs of Christchurch. Earlier that day I had been
at Canterbury University watching students mobilising with their shovels for another
hard day attacking the liquefaction. It brought  tears to my eyes because, along with the
Farmy Army, the students have shifted tonnes and tonnes of silt that was coverin g the
lawns and drives of so many householders who did not know what to do next. Much of
10 Mar 2011 Canterbury Earthquake Commemoration Day Bill 17137
the food that we were distributing on that day in Aranui was home-baked goodies. I was
particularly touched by a se t of buns covered with white icing. The person who had
baked them had taken the trouble to add lettering in pink ici ng to each bun, reading
simply “We love you”. That, to me, is the spirit of Christchurch today.
I agree with what Annette King said. We have to take time to grieve; we have to take
a breath. The memorial service on 18 March is  only part of the process; there is a lot
more to be done. Everyone in this House, particularly the Christchurch MPs—including
the Green MP Kennedy Graham—are doing their utmost to offer assistance. That is to
be commended. We are working very much in a cross-party spirit, as we should in such
a tragedy, and I think we will all be together next week on 18 March with the people of
Christchurch. Thank you.

items.speaker: TE URUROA FLAVELL
items.text: T ēnā koe, Mr Assistant
Speaker, kia ora t ātou katoa e te Whare, otir ā koutou e whakarongo mai n ā ki ngā
kōrero e pāoho atu nei ki a koutou i t ēnei rangi. Kātahi anō au ka whai wāhi ki te tū ake
ki te tuku i wā ku mihi, waku poroporoaki p ēnei i w ētahi atu i ng ā wiki kua hipi ake.
Kātahi anō au ka t ū ake ki te kī atu ki te hunga kua ngaro atu i te tirohanga kanohi, e
moe, e moe, e moe. Ko koutou t ērā ko te hunga i mate i Te Tai Poutini i ng ā marama
kua hipa ake. Haere koutou ki te wahang ūtanga. Haere koutou ki Hawaiki nui, ki
Hawaiki roa, ki Hawaiki p āmamao. Moe mai i roto i ng ā ringaringa o te w āhi ngaro mā
rātou kotuou e manaaki, e tiaki. Hoi anō ka hoki mai ki a tātou, ki a tātou e noho nei, m e
kī, ngā urupā o rātau mā, tēnā koutou, tēnā tātou katoa.
Ko tērā parekura nui i te 22 o Hui-tanguru kua tuhia ki roto i te ng ākau, i te wairua o
te tangata, me kī, o te motu o Aotearoa m ō ake nei. Āhua pērā tonu ki tērā hunga i mate
i raro i te whenua i Te Tai Poutini. Ko ētahi o te Whare nei kua tae atu ki te Ōtautahi.
Kua rongo koutou i te tangi. Kua rongo koutou i te mamae. Kua rongo koutou i te
āhuatanga o mate. Kua kite koutou i ng ā uauatanga, ng ā mamaetanga o t ēnā, o t ēnā, o
tēnā e noho mai rā ki tērā takiwā. Ko ahau, kāre anō kia tae atu. He mataku pea nōku, he
mataku pēnei nā, tērā pea mēnā ka haere au ki reira ka kite atu i ngā whare kua turakina.
Ka kite atu i te āhuatanga o ngā kaim ahi e kēri nei i te whenua kia kitea mai ai m ēnā he
tūpāpaku ki reira, tērā pea ka tangi.
Kāre e kore ka tangi, kia kite atu i tērā momo āhuatanga. Hoi anō, ka taea te whakatū
anō i tētahi whare hōu, ka taea te hoki ki te kura, ka taea te whaiwhai haere i ng ā taonga
i roto i ng ā whare engari, ko t āku noa ake, e kore pea te hunga e noho mai o roto o
Ōtautahi e kite i te pu āwaitanga o ng ā moemoeā kai mua i te aroaro, engari ko te mea
tino nui rawa atu, kua tau mai te āhuatanga o te mamae, o taumaha, o anip ā, o
āwangawanga ki runga i a rātau mō ake, ake nei. Koi nei te aroha atu.
Mēnā ka hoki mai au ki t ōku Ao M āori, arā nō ētahi kaupapa e k ōrerohia ana. Ko
tētahi, an ā kai te p ūtake o t ēnei pire. Ko te ingoa o t ērā tikanga, e kiia ana, ko te
poroporoaki. He aha te poroporoaki? He w ā e taea ana e te marea, e te marae ranei, e te
tangata rānei te tuku i t ōna ake k ōrero ki te hunga kua m ate. Ahakoa kotahi nei, he ika
hui rua r ānei, he parekura rā nei. Koi nei te āhuatanga o te poroporoaki. Ko t ā te
poroporoaki, he whiu i te kupu k ōrero ki runga i te tangata, he whakah ē i a ia i ētahi wā
engari ko te nuinga o te w ā, he whakanui i a ia. He whakanui i ng ā mea kua kitea nei,
kua rangona nei e te nuinga. He w ā ka whai w āhi ngā tamariki ki te tuku i ētahi kōrero
tērā pea, kāore i kōrerohia i te wā i a rātou e ora ana, e takatū ana i te mata o te whenua.
He wā kia heke te roimata, heke i te kanohi nei, ng ā pāpāringa o te tangata, an ā mā
ēnei tohu o te hūpē me te roimata, i kōrerohia mai nā e te Hōnore Pita Sharples, ka āhua
ngāwari mai te āhuatanga o tē nei mea o te mate. Engari, ko te 18 o ng ā rā o t ēnei
marama, k ātahi te tangihanga ko t ērā. He tangihanga nui, whakaharahara m ō te m otu
whānui tonu. N ō reira, ko tāku pātai ki a t ātau, pēhea e taea ai e te motu te whakanui
rānei, te whaiwhai haere r ānei i t ēnei mea o te poroporoaki i te mea, ar ā ānō ētahi
17138 Canterbury Earthquake Commemoration Day Bill 10 Mar 2011
raruraru p ēnei t ā te H ōnore Trevor Mallard i k ōrero mai n ā, in ā tata nei. P ēnei i tā
Hōnore Annette King, p ēnei an ō rā i tā  Keith Locke i te mea, ar ā an ō ngā  raruraru.
Tuatahi, ko te tangata nei ko Joseph P ōhio, nō tērā takiwā. Ko ia t ērā i t ō mai i t ētahi
wahine, ki taku m ōhio, ā, i te w ā o te r ū. Nā, kite mai ai tana tinana, tana t ūpāpaku kua
tukuna nā tana marae a ia i poroporoaki, kua t āpukengia ki te whenua, kua hoki an ō rā
ki a Papatūānuku. Ko ia tētahi i mahi nei i roto i te civil defence , e ai ki taku m ōhio mō
ngā 21 tau hipa noa atu. Pēhea e taea ai te tuku roimata i te mea kua ea tērā?
Pēhea mō ngā mātua o te pēpi nei o Taneysha?  E rima wiki noa iho tana pakeke. M ō
Baxter? E rima marama noa iho tōna pakeke. He pēpi, kāre i kite i te puāwaitanga o ngā
moemoeā, kāore i kite i te ao. Me p ēhea hoki te tuku i te roimata m ō te hunga pakeke,
koeke, koroua r ānei, kuia rā nei? E ai ki ng ā kōrero, ko Stuart r āua Lucy Routledge. He
whaiāipō i a rā ua e tamariki ana, 50 tau r āua e noho tahi ana. T ērā pea ko Maureen
Fletcher? Pērā anō hoki tērā kuia, e ai ki taku rongo. E hia k ē nei ngā ingoa, e hia kē nei
ngā maumaharatanga. Kua turakinatia katoatia ērā āhuatanga katoa. Me p ēhea e taea ai
e tātau te whakatau i tērā hunga te kāhui kua ngaro atu i te tirohanga kanohi.
Ko tāku, ko te mihi ki ng ā kaipāpāho e ngana nei, m e kī, ki te pā oho i ng ā kōrero o
tēnā, o tēnā o te hunga kua ngaro. Nā rātou anō rā te kōrero mō Jaime Gilbert. Ko ia tērā
i mate nei me tana m ōhio, i te ora tana ta na tuahine. Ko t ā rātou ko t ā te kaip āpāho, he

Ko t āku pā tai, e p ēnei ana. Me p ēhea te hunga k āore an ō kia whakahokia ki ng ā

Koia nei kai te p ūtake o te k ōrero a te H ōnore a Trevor Mallard. P ēhea e

kai t ēnā, kai t ēnā, kai t ēnā. He uaua te tuku i te mamae, i te roimata, i te h ūpē mēnā
karekau tēta
hi i reira. Nō reira, me whai whakaaro tātou mō ērā.
Ka mutu, he hunga an ō o tāwāhi, he pērā anō te āhua. I rongo au i te reo irirangi, ko

mate ki a Hinenuitepō. Ko tāku e kī nei, mahia te mahi, kāre he hē o te whaiwhai haere i
ēnei āhuatanga katoa engari, m
e whai tātou mō te hunga k āre anō kia kite i ō rātou ake
tūpāpaku.
I kōrerohia mō te āhuatanga o tēnei mea o te r āhui. Ko te r āhui, he momo taiapa kia
kore te tangata e haere ki reira pēnei i ngā taiapa i te tāone o Ōtautahi i tēnei wā. He aha
te tikanga o te r āhui? Kia waiho ki t ōna āhua. Kia kaua e p ā atu. I te ngahere, ka
waihotia kia tipu, kia pu āwai an ō rā ngā  kai. M ō te rā hui o te hunga kua ngaro, kia
waiho ake, kia noho i runga i te āhuatanga o te tapu. He w ā tōna, ka whakanoatia kia

Ka mutu, ko taku kōrero whakamutunga, kia whai w āhi anō rā ko te ā huatanga o te
karakia, kia whakang āwari i te noho i Ō tautahi me te m ōhio an ō hoki, k āre an ō ētahi
tinana k
ia kitea noa. Mā te karakia pea, ka whakang āwari mai ai te noho o ērā tūpāpaku
ki reira. Nō reira, ko tā mātau, he tautoko, he tautoko engari, te t ūmanako ia kua rongo i
te tikanga o ēnei kōrero, kaua ki te whakahāwea engari, ki te kī atu, arā anō ētahi take e
noho tārewa āna. Huri noa i tō tātau Whare, kia ora tātou.
10 Mar 2011 Canterbury Earthquake Commemoration Day Bill 17139
[Greetings, Mr Assistant Speaker, and the H ouse, and to those listening in today to
this broadcast. This is my first opportunity to offer up  words and farewells as others
have done in these weeks past. This is my  first opportunity to stand here and say to
those who died, rest in peace; abide with those who perished in the disaster on the West
Coast mere months ago, your voices hereafte r mute. Depart to grea t Hawaiki, to long
Hawaiki, to distant Hawaiki. Rest in the wo rld of the spirits who are to care and tend
you. Returning here, to us, as we sit here—the remnants, so to speak—I greet us all.
The disaster that fell on 22 February has for ever left an indelible mark on the hearts
and the souls of the people of Aotearoa. Its ef fect was similar to the mining disaster on
the West Coast. Some of the members of this House have visited Christchurch. You
heard the lamentations. You sensed the pai n. You felt the foreboding of death. You saw
the effects of the disaster and the pain borne by the individuals of  the region. I myself
have not yet gone there. Perhaps I am fear ful of going, lest I see the collapsed
buildings, lest I witness the rescue workers digging throug h the rubble, searching for
bodies, and lament.
Having to look upon those sights, I have no doubt that that is what would happen.
Buildings can be rebuilt, students can in time return to school, and household
possessions can eventually be replaced. I maintain, however, that the people of
Christchurch will never see their dreams  realised, and pain, darkness, worry, and
anxiety will be a permanent companion. For this, I extend my love.
Allow me to turn to aspects of my M āori World, Mr Assistant Speaker, and speak of
things therein that here pertain. One of those aspects or customs is at the heart of this
bill. That custom is poroporoaki. What is poroporoaki? Poroporoaki is the opportunity
given for the multitude, or individuals, usually at a marae, to speak to the departed. It
matters not whether one person is lying in state, or two, or many deaths due to disaster.
In a poroporoaki, words of fa rewell are offered to the deceased. There are times when
harsh words may be uttered, but most speeches extol the virtues of the deceased, the
good that people saw and heard. Often an opport unity is given for young people to say
farewell, perhaps share things they never said to the person when he or she was alive.
This is a time for acknowledging loss and expressing our grief. For it is the shedding
of tears and mucus referred to by the Hon Pita  Sharples that alleviates some of the pain
caused by death. Come the 18th day of this month, we will grieve; the whole country will
be in mourning. So my question is, how c an the nation appropriate ly acknowledge and
be engaged in the farewell to the dead? Fo r as the Hon Trevor Mallard only recently
stated, there are difficulties. The Hon A nnette King and Keith Locke have also raised
concerns. How do we pay our respects to them? How do we pay our respects to Joseph
Pōhio of Christchurch? During the earthquake he dragged a woman away from danger.
When his body was found it was taken to his marae to be mourned, then interred in the
bosom of the earth. I understand he had worked for civil de fence for 21 years. How can
we mourn this one if it has already been done?
And what of the parents of baby Tan eysha? She was only 5 weeks old. What about
Baxter? He was only 5 months old. Those were babies who never got the chance to
enjoy life. So many families are bereft, left without the wisdom and cultural heritage of
their elders—Stuart and Lucy Routledge, childhood sweethearts, married for over 50
years; grandmother Maureen Fletcher, ever remembered for her uplifting spirit—so
many names and memories and shattered dreams that we in this House cannot possibly
do justice to.
I want to acknowledge the media for trying to record the stories of the dead. They
told us about Jaime Gilbert, w ho died with a smile on his fa ce, knowing that his sister
was out of harm’s way. They have accurately recorded this tragedy so that the people of
the country and the world can know the calamity that has befallen Aotearoa.
17140 Canterbury Earthquake Commemoration Day Bill 10 Mar 2011

items.speaker: I pose this question
items.text: what of the dead w ho have not yet been returned to their
grieving families? The families are waiting for the release of their loved ones. How can
one grieve for the dead if there is no body to address? That is at the heart of the address
by the Hon Trevor Mallard: how can the appropriate words be said if there is no body?
That conflicts with M āoridom, for it is only when the deceased is lying in state in the
meeting house that observations and farewells  can be made. So in these circumstances,
how can M āori acquit their customs, their lamentations, their mourning, their songs,
their oratory?
I acknowledge that others have their own cu stoms and practices. It  is difficult to
release the pain, the tears, and the mucus if there is no body. Think about that.
Foreigners were also victims of the eart hquake. I heard the media make mention of
Japanese students who lost their lives. The Japanese have their own rituals and customs
surrounding death, somewhat similar to M āori. They await the return of their loved
ones to them. I listened to the comments on the proposed day of commemoration, and
agree; yes it is a very significant occa sion, it should proceed, and it should be
supported by all. But some say that perhaps  it is too early to hold a commemoration;
accusations of moving with indecent haste to bury the dead are being made. I say, carry
on with the task in hand. There is nothing wrong with carrying on with these
proceedings, but give all support to those who still await the return of the bodies of
their loved ones to them.
I turn now to the term “ r āhui”. That term refers to a ki nd of fence or barricade that
prevents people from entering, similar to  the warning fences around parts of
Christchurch. What is the purpose of rāhui? Things are left alone, untouched. In the
forest, r āhui allows for regeneration and pr otection of food sources. For rāhui in
relation to the dead, let it remain in pl ace, sacred. At the right time the r āhui will be
removed, and the grieving will settle.
And finally, has space been a fforded for the appropriate prayers to be given to give
succour to Christchurch, in th e knowledge that there are still bodies not yet recovered?
Prayers may help to bring pe ace to those still buried un der the rubble. We are in
support. But we hope that our words are heed ed, not to be taken as criticism, but to
bring to the attention of a ll that some matters still need addressing. So to us all
throughout our House, thank you.]

items.speaker: JO GOODHEW
items.text: As I rise to sp eak on the Canterbury
Earthquake Commemoration Day Bill, I need to  record my heartfelt sympathy to those
who have suffered great loss as a result of the 22 February earthquake. Loss has come in
many forms: loss of loved ones—and with that, loss of future dreams and plans—loss of
homes and possessions, loss of businesses and jobs, and loss of what we knew to be the
Christchurch we lived in, worked in, and visited. Here I must add an acknowledgment
to those from overseas who are also mourning lost ones, and for some of them lost jobs,
as well.
This tragedy became international from the moment it happened. Reports of the
earthquake sped rapidly around the world, and within minutes we were receiving texts
and emails from people asking whether we we re OK. Some of those texts and emails
were never received, and no reply with good news will ever be received, either. In a
modern world with communication tools ap lenty, being out of communication causes
