immeasurable anxiety, particularly at a tim e like this. After the earthquake, cellphones
helped to save lives, they helped to bring aid to those in need, and they brought good
news to m
any, as well. We all looked at t hose texts with relief in  our hearts. But the
silence of cellphones when answers were sought was unnerving and worrying, and in
the end hinted at sorrow and loss.
10 Mar 2011 Canterbury Earthquake Commemoration Day Bill 17141
Although there has been great loss, co rrespondingly, great courage has been
displayed and tremendous generosity exhibite d. Again, the internatio nal nature of this
event has marked its gravity. Incredibly ra pidly, nations from ar ound the world offered
their assistance, and New Zealand, as a nati on, said “Thank you. Yes, we do need your
help.” We are a generous nation when it come s to offering our expertise to others in
strife, so it was no great surprise that it was reciprocated. It was no surprise;
nevertheless, it was a huge comfort to know that the numbers of our incredibly skilled
emergency personnel and our urban search an d rescue people were to be massively
swelled by ranks of Aussies, Singaporeans, Brits, Americans, Taiwanese, Chinese, and
Japanese. We welcomed them with open arms.
Emergency services people in fluoro vests and in uniform brought enormous comfort
to a nation on edge, as we hoped against hope that more lives could be saved in the
aftermath of the earthquake. The courage of those who have  been searching will spawn
heart-warming and emotional stor ies that will become part of this nation’s history. The
early searchers were actually the people w ho were caught up in the earthquake. They
displayed sometimes superhuman efforts as they freed trapped people. We heard of
despair, elation, hope, and tragedy.
We must acknowledge the media and the way they brought this event into our lives
through all of their mediums. At times the s cenes of destruction became too much, the
bad news unendurable, and we turned them—the  media—off. But, really, we could not
escape the reality of what the Christchurch  people were living through, so the question
became what we were going to do in res ponse. Everywhere—again, not just in New
Zealand but also internationally—the questions were “What can we do?” and “What
should we do to help?”. I have witnessed a nd spoken to people who have become quite
agitated because they personally could not th ink of a way they could physically help.
But over time we have worked out ways to help—each of us in our own way.
The armies of all shapes, sizes, and descriptions were there, mobilised. Our own
armed forces, which so fortuitously were  in Canterbury on an exercise, were in
Christchurch very quickly. Then we had th e Student Volunteer Army, the Farmy Army,
the Salvation Army, the other church groups that mobilised their own armies of helpers,
the army of Government departments that swung their plans of support into action, the
health army, the armies of businesses that looked to fill every need their own expertise
could offer, and the skilled and generous armies of volunteers w ho man every welfare
centre and take aid to those in need.
On Friday, 18 March we will commemorate the ev ent, and it is fair to say that in my
electorate of Rangitata there is a mixed reaction to the public holiday. The businesses in
mid-Canterbury are concerned at the financ ial impact this unexpected public holiday
will have on them. The decision to commemo rate the event with a public holiday was
not made without all the parties of Parlia ment considering its financial impact. The
proposal the Government put to the other parties, and to which they have agreed, was to
allow people, through the memorial service, to have a day on which to reflect upon the
event and to be amongst their loved ones, family, and community.
In South Canterbury, the southern part of  my electorate, where people identify very
closely with Christchurch and with their friends and families there and who feel like
close neighbours of Christchurch, there is no public holiday, and some are not happy
about that. Nevertheless, there will be an opportunity for them to mark the
commemoration with reflection. It is my hope  that through the memorial service in
Christchurch and the planned services at lunchtime in Timaru and at 9.30 a.m. in
Ashburton, our people can gather together to mourn, to pay tribute, and to gather their
energies for the future. It is my hope that the day will be a day for reflection, tribu tes,
and a strong sense of community and purpose.
17142 Canterbury Earthquake Commemoration Day Bill 10 Mar 2011
As our Prime Minister has said, we will stand shoulder to shoulder with the people of
Christchurch and their loved ones. We will al so stand shoulder to shoulder with those
from other nations who have experienced lo ss. Our support, shoulder to shoulder, will
not need to be just for today, tomorrow, a nd next week; it will be required for months
and years to come. The people of Christchur ch may doubt their strength when in the
depths of despair, but they are gaining in  strength, as are thei r neighbours in wider
Canterbury. The strength of the nation wi ll be from strong shoulders to help
Christchurch in the days, weeks, months, and years to come. Thank you.

items.speaker: DARIEN FENTON
items.text: It is a privilege to take a call on the Canterbury
Earthquake Commemoration Day Bill. I start by paying my respects to all those who
have lost their lives, to their families, to all those who have been injured, to all those
who are still struggling just to  get along in their homes, and to all those who have lost
homes. Just the sheer enormity of this disa ster, I think, has been a shock for all of us,
even those who, like me, have not been to Christchurch since the tragedy. I think that all
of us throughout New Zealand have been st ruggling to come to terms with this
horrendous event.
I also acknowledge all of the Ministers, a nd particularly the Minister of Labour, who
I know lives in Christchurch. I thank her for bringing this bill to the House. Even
though we have some reservations—very small ones—about the timing of it, we think it
is a very good gesture, and an appropriate one in the circumstances.
There is genuine grief and sadness throughout  the country. It will last for some time
to come, and there will be many times in the future also when people will need support.
They need it now, but they w ill continue to need it. We must make sure that the
commemoration day commemorates those who lost their lives and takes care of the
families that are suffering. But also we must look to the future and continue to work
together to help rebuild Christchurch.
It affects us all. We are all in this toge ther, and all of those who live today will not
forget it easily or quickly. My grandfather was in the Napier earthquake, and he talked
about it a lot. He was a minist er of religion at the time, and he had to immediately leave
his family of four and help his parishione rs. My father, who was just a little boy, relates
the story that he was at sc hool and was walking away from  a building when he turned
round and saw an enormous crevice behind him. He ended up with a little ticket, almost
like a refugee ticket, that helped him ge t access to food and other things. Both my
grandfather and father were enormously aff ected by that earthquake. Both of them had
been through world wars, but the earthquake was the thing they talked about much more
when we talked about tragedies and the awful things that had happened in their
lifetimes.
I think the commemoration day is an appropriate response to the trag edy. I dedicate
the words in my first reading speech this afternoon to the workers of Canterbury. Many
of the people that were killed or injured were just ordinary wo rking people who were
going about their jobs. It was tragic that it happened at lunchtime. Some had stepped
outside and gone to lunch, and were caught in  Cashel Mall, and others had just come
back from lunch and had just got back in to their buildings when their buildings
collapsed. They were just people who went to work in the morning, said goodbye to
their families, and were never seen again. That is utterly heartbreaking. We mourn all of
those workers—the dead, the injured, and th e lost—but also we mourn with all the
people who are affected.
I also acknowledge all the workers that have been at the forefront of the rescue effort
in Christchurch, and I thank the Minister of Police for her contribution today. It is pretty
gruelling stuff to listen to, and it must be even more gruelling to be working on the front
line, retriev
ing the lost, and trying to get them back to their families. It is a pretty
10 Mar 2011 Canterbury Earthquake Commemoration Day Bill 17143
gruesome job, and I thank them for being ther e to do that. An important part of families
being able to have closure is getting their loved ones home and saying goodbye to them.
Of course, there were firefighters and rescue  workers, health wo rkers, social support
workers, education workers, and community wo rkers. An enormous effort has been put
in by the working people of Christchurch, and, indeed, around the country. People have
mentioned, for example, Ministry of Social Development workers. I tried to contact my
local Ministry of Social Development o ffice in Northcote th e other day, and the
message was that they were all working on  Christchurch. That is fair enough; I
understand that. It just shows us the effort that is being put in, and I really appreciate it.
When Helen Clark, our previous Prime Minister, visited Christchurch, she said it was
worse than Haiti. I am sure it is worse in te rms of devastation, but what is not worse is
the fact that we live in a country that is a democrac y, has great public services, has a
Government and a Parliament that are able to work together, and is wealthy enough to
get through this—and we will get through this. We do not have to witness the dreadful
post-earthquake scenes we saw in Haiti.
There are many stories, which will emerge in the weeks to come, of workers who
were absolute heroes. Let me say that I am not talking about just workers—I know there
were many heroes—but I particularly want to  talk about them. I heard of workers who
helped workmates out through the rubble and over the bricks, a nd who put their own
lives at risk to help people they were working with. Thousands of workers have
volunteered, along with the rest of the community, to help in  a variety of ways, despite
their own losses. They may have lost a loved one or be missing someone, they may
have lost their homes, and they may be living in absolute devastation.
Caregivers helped relocate hundreds of older people from aged-care facilities to other
parts of the country. Can members imagine what it was like for those who live with
disabilities, particularly those with intellectual disabilities who are living in their family
home? It would have been caregivers who comforted them and looked after them.
Nurses rolled up their sleeves  and went off to work. Th ey reported for duty and got
stuck in, as, of course, did doctors.
As I said, I think it is really appropriate that we set aside a day to mourn the losses,
and it is appropriate that it is a public holiday, because there is no other way we can be
sure that the workers of Christchurch will be able to attend—there is no other way. As
others have said, we have some questions about whether it is the right time, but I do not
want to go into that too much at the moment. Like my colleague Trevor Mallard, I want
to ensure that the front-line workers—polic e officers, health workers, and rescue
workers—are able to attend. I feel a little concerned that they will be needed elsewhere,
and I would appreciate the coope ration of the Government in  trying to get the message
through that it is very important  for those workers to attend, because it is for them as
much as anyone else. Imagine what they ha ve witnessed and what  they have been
through in the last couple of weeks.
There are consequences, of c ourse, of the earthquake. I do not want to go into them
too much, but thousands of workers are now out of a job. A lot of businesses no longer
exist, and many are on the margins. I think th ere will be questions about that as we go
through the next few weeks.
While I have the opportunity I want to sa y that the Governme nt’s response, its
emergency package, was far more generous th an last time, and I know it has been taken
up by tens of thousands. I think that someth ing like $50 m illion has been given out so
far, and I congratulate the Government on th at. There are some other issues around that
response package. I do not inte nd to go into them now; maybe I will a little later in the
debate.
17144 Canterbury Earthquake Commemoration Day Bill 10 Mar 2011
I reiterate my genuine sorrow and sadness ab out this dreadful event and give my
aroha to the people of Canterbury, to the pe ople in this House who are suffering, and to
all of us in New Zealand, who will have to stand together to get through this.

items.speaker: Hon TAU HENARE
items.text: Te mea tuatahi, ki ng ā mōrehu, ki ngā  wh ānau
pani o te r ū whenua o Ōtautahi, ka nui taku mihi me taku aroha ki a koutou katoa. Ki
ngā mate o te parekura nei, haere atu r ā, haere atu rā, haere atu rā. He wā potopoto tēnei
mihimihi, he w ā potopoto t ēnei aroha ki a r ātou engari, nunui ta ku mihi, nunui taku
aroha ki a rātou katoa i roto i te rohe pōtae o Ngāi Tahu.
He pātai tāku ki taku hoa, ki taku tuakana a Te Ur uroa. He aha te kaupapa, he aha te
tikanga mō te rā  e heke mai nei ā te 18? N ō te mea, k āore tērā rā he r ā nehu. Harakau
ngā tūpāpaku i mua i a m ātou nō reira, p ātai ai ki a koutou katoa i roto i te rangim ārie.
He aha te tikanga, he aha te kaupapa o te rā  nei? Ki ahau nei, he whakamaumahara, he
whakahōnore i ngā mōrehu, i ngā tūpāpakui rānei i Ōtautah i. Kāore he rā nehu.
[First of all, my immense sympathy and admiration to you all, the survivors and
grieving families of the Christchurch earthqua ke. In regard to those who died in this
disaster, I bid you farewell, goodbye, j ourney on. While this acknowledgment and
tribute is a very, very brief one, my so rrow and regard to all of them in the Ng āi Tahu
region is immense.
I have a question to my fellow member and senior relative Te Ururoa. What is the
thinking and meaning behind the coming 18th? Because it is not a burial day. Those who
died will not be lying in state before us. So I ask this of you all, with respect and without
malice. What is the purpose and meaning of this day? To me, it is a day to
commemorate and honour the survivors or those from Christchurch who died. It is not a
burial day.]
I have been trying to figure out in wh ich box to put 18 March. I for one am not
concerned about the day itself, but I am concerned about the significance, the tikanga,
and the protocol behind it all. To me it is not  right and it is not wrong; my own personal
point of view is that 18 March is a time to commemorate not only those who lost their
lives but also those who surv ived, and those who assisted with the recovery and the
rescue. It is a day to honour all of those people of Christchurch. I am a fan of history, so
I have looked very hard at Napier over the years. I have looked at all sorts of incidents
that have happened in our world over the last  100-odd years. But in my room at 10 to 1
on that fateful day, I could not help but be transfixed and heartbroken at what I was
seeing.
I also say that that day will become a day for the people of Christchurch, who,
regardless of their own personal circumstances, have reached out to strangers and to
people they would not even say hello to on a normal day. It shows the strength of
Christchurch and of the people in Christchur ch, of people in New Zealand, and also of
people around the world, that we can actually assist and help each other in a time of
need.
I commend the Canterbury Earthquake Commem oration Day Bill to the House. It is
unfortunate that we have to use the word “holiday”—ehara i te hararei—but it is the
only word that allows us—

items.speaker: Hon Trevor Mallard
items.text: “Holy day”—pronounce it the old way.

items.speaker: Hon TAU HENARE
items.text: I do not believe that it is a hol y day. I do not believe that it is
a holy day; I think it is a special day, a commemorative day. T ērā te tikanga o te rā  nei,
ki ahau nei. Kaua e pāpōuri ki tōku nei whakaaro.
[That is what that day means to me—and do not be disappointed.]
I commend the bill to the House. I think it  is appropriate that  we commemorate all
those people who have been involved, who have been hit, and who have been hurt by
this huge event that will live long in our memories as we go on.
10 Mar 2011 Canterbury Earthquake Commemoration Day Bill 17145
I give my special regards to Ng āi Tahu and to all of the iwi who have rallied around
and sent health teams. The brother-in-law has kept me informed of what Tainui has
been doing, so I congratulate Tainui. I congr atulate Te Arawa, Raukawa, and all of
those iwi who have seen fit to send teams of  helpers to Christchurch to help not only
Ngāi Tahu but also their wh ānau. It shows that iwi can actually help each other in their
time of need, as well.
Hoi an ō, an ō taku mihi, an ō taku aroha ki a r ātou, ki ō r ātou mamae, ki ō
rātouāwangawanga hoki. Nō reira, tēnā koutou, ā, tēnā koutou, kia ora mai tātou katoa.
[So my sympathy and admiration again to th em, for their pains and concerns, as
well. Greetings to you, greetings to you, and to us all.]

items.speaker: CHARLES CHAUVEL
items.text: It is an honour to have an opportunity to speak
in the debate on the Canterbury Earthquake Commemoration Day Bill. As others before
me have done, I begin by acknowledging the people of Christchurch and Canterbury,
and in particular those who have died or who have been injured, and their families and
friends. I also echo the words of appreciation that have already been said in the House
about the work of the emergency services —both the workers in  the domestic New
Zealand services and also all of those from  overseas who have come to assist New
Zealand in its hour of need. There would not be one person in the Chamber who has not
been moved by that extraordinary gesture of support that was so quickly forthcoming
and so reassuring. It almost seemed as if we did not need to ask. The help was there and
it has been, and is, magnificent. I know that the police and others have been incredibly
impressed by the level of the support they have been able to call on, and have also said
what a difference it has made in practice on the ground. I do not thi nk that we, as MPs,
can do enough to stress just how important that support has been.
Obviously, it is also appr opriate to acknowledge all th e many New Zealanders who
have volunteered in many ways—through fund-raising or their own labour, and through
donating cakes at the bake-off in Auckland th e other day—or who have simply got on
with providing assistance in whatever way they have been able to. The importance of
what we are doing today by moving to enact this bill, I think, is to acknowledge all
those people, and to say that we want to do something concrete by way of
demonstrating appreciation as well as doing the appropriate thing to remember all those
who have been so devastated by the event itself.
I had a family member in Christchurch on the day of the quake. For my family and
me it was an anxious time while we waited to  hear about her safet y. She told us just
how terrifying it was to be in the quake itsel f. She managed to get under a table when it
started, and when she got out from under the table after the earthquake, she saw that a
bookcase had fallen right on to the chair she had been sitting on and crushed it. She then
described just how awful it was to be ther e for another 24 hours, hearing the roaring
sound of the aftershocks. I know that Canter bury m
embers who have experienced this
must have found that it really wears them do wn on a daily basis. It was hard enough to
hear about a family member being trapped in it for a day. The sense of relief that we felt
when she arrived back in Wellington was extr aordinary. If that is what it feels like to
have a connection on that sort of intimate level for 24 hours, it must be much more
harrowing to be living this day to day in Canterbury and participa ting in the recovery
efforts.
I also acknowledge a staff member of  mine who moved to Wellington from
Christchurch last year, and who has family and friends still down there. I have seen
firsthand what she has gone through, in te rms of finding out about loved ones affected
by the quake and about people close to her w ho have died. Again, it is not a firsthand
experience, but it gives some insight into just what people in Canterbury are going
17146 Canterbury Earthquake Commemoration Day Bill 10 Mar 2011
through at the moment. It makes it doubly appropr iate, I think, for us to be mindful of
those experiences while we have this debate today.
Of course, other memorial services have already been held acr oss the nation, and I
speak in particular of the ones that were held on 1 March. There was the service here on
the steps of Parliament, which was organise d by the Anglican Cathedral next door, and
in which a number of other fa iths participated. It was a real privilege to be able to
participate in that service on behalf of colleagues. The deputy leader of the Labour Party
has said previously that it is appropriate that  it has been agreed that the procedure to be
followed on 18 March is that partisanship wi ll be set aside and there will be speakers
from across the House. That is absolutely right. These affairs ought to be ones where we
can participate as a Parliament in a solemn  and non-political occas ion. I hope that that
will always be the convention in respect of these sorts of matters. We should not even
have to ask about them; it should be second nature that these events are held in this way.
In respect of the present b ill, I do not think that anybody disagrees with the absolute
appropriateness of a day of commemoration, a day of honouring the work that has been
done already in relation to the Canterbury recovery. I am not sure how the House will
progress this debate—or whether there will be a traditional Committee stage where the
Minister will discuss any issues concerning  the bill. Depending on how we proceed, it
might be appropriate to ask her a couple of  questions about what is planned. I will
foreshadow a couple of issues now that I hope she might be able to have a think about.
Whether we have a Committee stage or whet her the Minister chooses to deal with
questions in her second or third reading speeches, I am happy either way.
Obviously there has been a concern about timing. A lot of people in Canterbury are
still engaged in the recovery  and clean-up. There are still lots of people without power,
sewerage, or water, and we know that all effort is being put into prioritising the
restoration of those services. We know how important that is, but will the
commemoration day be too soon for some of the people working in essential services,
the people who have contributed in the aftermath:  police officers, civil defence staff,
fire brigades, doctors and nurses, other he alth workers, drainlayers, contractors,
demolition crews, and many others? It would just be fantastic to be assured that
appropriate provision will be made so that  everybody who wants to come together to
participate in the service on 18 March will have the opportunity  to take a little bit of
respite from the dreadful recovery work and have the opportunity to do that.
Of course there are the 70,000 people who have already left Canterbury, and who are
only just beginning to think about whether th ey can return. It would be good to know
that the Government has thought about thei r position, as well. Obviously people who
have had to leave but want to come back and be part of the commemoration process
need to be considered, as well.
I do not think there is any doubt about the appropriateness of a public holiday. I do
not think we should be concerned about the economics. I had a call from one of the MPs
in Christchurch today who was working with a delicatessen in Lyttelton that has had to
move premises. The owners need to apply for a new licence because they serve wine.
They were told by the city council that if they applied for a new licence it would be
opposed, because the policy now is that delicat essens are not the ideal place to serve
wine. W
ell, that is the sort of red tape we need to cut through, ra ther than worry about
whether we should be having a public holiday and the effects of that. With those words
I congratulate the Government on moving to  a commemoration, and I commend the bill
to the House.

items.speaker: DAVID BENNETT
items.text: I follow on from all the speakers
in the House today, and, I am sure, all the members of the House and the wider New
Zealand community, in paying respect to the people of Christchurc h, their family and
10 Mar 2011 Canterbury Earthquake Commemoration Day Bill 17147
friends, and all those involved in the resc ue efforts from New Zealand and around the
world. The spirit of the Canterbury people has shown resilience and a desire to be
strong in these times, and the wider New Zealand public has shown tremendous feeling
and respect for the people of Christchurch and Canterbury an d the desire to help where
they can.
A lot of what has been done and is being done is quite symbolic , in the sense of
sharing emotions and grief. That symbolis m is also very important to people going
through the situation in Christchurch, who know that they have support and
comradeship, and that they are in the thoughts and feelings of all New Zealanders.
The Canterbury Earthquake Commemoration Day Bill enshrines another aspect of
symbolism of the support that New Zealanders ar e willing to show at this time. It sets
aside a holiday for the people of Christchurch and Canterbury in commemoration of the
devastating consequences of the earthquake. It  will be a symbol for that region of what
people have endured, and also, I am sure, a sy mbol of what they want to achieve and
rebuild. Such a symbol will be followed by people throughout New Zealand also, and, I
guess, around the world, by New Zealanders overseas, who wish to pay tribute and wish
to support the country and the people of Canterbury at this time.
Speaking as one of the members from outsi de the Canterbury region, I express that
our thoughts and our feelings are with the pe ople of Canterbury a nd Christchurch. We
look forward to this day as a way to s how that support, so that the people of
Christchurch know that they are supported an d that New Zealanders are together and
with each other in showing respect for the people of Christchurch at this time. I
commend the bill to the House.
Bill read a first time.
Second Reading

items.speaker: Hon KATE WILKINSON
items.text: I move, That the Canterbury
Earthquake Commemoration Day Bill be now read a second time . As we have said, this
bill provides for 18 March 2011 to be a day of commemoration in those parts of
Canterbury that observe Chri stchurch Show Day as Canterbury Anniversary Day, in
order to commemorate the devastating cons equences of the Canterbury earthquake on
22 February 2011 at 12.51 p.m. It is a day an d a time that will, I think, be indelibly
etched on all our minds for many, many years and decades to come.
This day will be treated as a public holiday , with schools require d to close for the
purposes of the Education Act. There is no restriction on shop trading. Businesses will
be able to continue trading on the day, if th ey choose to. The significance of having a
public holiday on Friday, 18 March is to prov ide people with an opportunity to attend
the memorial service for the victims of the 22 February earthquake.
A couple of issues were raised in some of the first reading speeches, and as a
Cantabrian I thank all members of the Hous e for the compassion, the feelings, and the
concern expressed for Canterbury and Christchurch. Christchurch is my home town and,
as many will know, I am a pretty proud Cantab rian. One of the issues was whether it
should be a national public holiday or a regional public holiday. It was considered more
appropriate that it be a pr ovincial holiday. It is an im portant day of mourning for
Canterbury and is very personal for the region. That is not, however, to diminish its
national importance, and, indeed, also its international importance.
Economically, it is also important that the rest of the country can continue working,
as this will assist Canterbury and the Canter bury rebuild. It is certainly hoped that many
people throughout the country outside Canterbur y will at least be able to watch the
service from afar so that they, in their own place and in their own way, can mourn. They
17148 Canterbury Earthquake Commemoration Day Bill 10 Mar 2011
can pay tribute, contemplate the utter trage dy of what happened, build strength, and use
that strength to help Cantab rians and New Zealanders on the long road ahead for the
rebuild and recovery.
I also acknowledge one of the previous speakers who referred to the timing and
asked why we are holding a provincial holiday on 18 March. I am not sure that there is
ever a right time for such a commemoration. For some, undeniably, it will be too soon;
for some it may be too late; and for some it is about right. But we hope that it is
appropriate for Cantabrians to join together on that day and to know they are not alone.
We are there with them, shoulder to shoul der, as a province and a nation, and as a
Parliament, to help them down the long road of recovery and rebuild. It will be a chance
to reflect on the terrible loss of life suffered as a result of the earthquake and the
massive impact it has had on our second-largest city.
It is also an opportu nity to give thanks for the ci vil defence services, by which I
mean the volunteers, the community, the frie nds, the family, and the professionals. All
were out there working with one thought in mind, and that was the welfare of
Cantabrians and Christchurch people and of th e visitors who had been so unfortunately
caught up in such a tragic even t. I think we can have some pride in the resilience of our
communities when we have our professionals—the police, nurses, doctors, civil defence
professionals, and search and rescue wo rkers—and volunteers all out there with no
thought at all for their own homes, which we re also shattered and in tatters in many
cases.
This is an opportunity for the people of Ca nterbury to mourn together. We consider
that providing a one-off public holiday for the people of northern and central
Canterbury to allow them this opportunity to attend a memorial service is an appropriate
response in these truly difficult times. I commend this bill to the House.

items.speaker: Hon TREVOR MALLARD
items.text: I indicate again, without any
surprise, that Labour will support the sec ond reading of the Canterbury Earthquake
Commemoration Day Bill, and will suppor t the bill going through tonight. I
acknowledge the speeches that were made afte r mine. I know that is slightly unusual
after the first reading. In pa rticular, I commend the eloquent speech my colleague Mr
Flavell made. He expressed much of  what he said as being for M āori, but I think much
of what he said applies to all New Zeala nders. The importance of having the dead to
commemorate and memorialise is important. He made some comments about the timing
of the commemoration, and getting that right. Although we are heading for a
parliamentary, unified outcome, in the end the date is the Government’s decision. We
understand that a certain amount of the timi ng has been driven by the availability of
international visitors, so we acknowledge th at and we accept that this is going to
happen.
But I think this leaves us with a question about what happens later. I think we should
take time—months, or even years—to decide how we want to remember this occasion. I
will also mention Pike River, because proportionately, in community size, that was an
enormous tragedy too. I hate to think of putti ng labels on tragedy, but it is almost like
we will have to make some sort of me morial arrangements for the South Island
tragedies of 2010 and 2011. It may be that peop le with better linguistic skills than mine
can develop a label for that, and we can head towards some sort of commemoration on a
regular basis. As I said ear lier, I think too often we th ink of physical commemorations,
and we have to find ways of thinking more deeply than that. I indicate to the Minister of
Labour that she might have a bit of work to  do in Christchurch. I have just seen a
comment that has come through from local  business people who have som e anxiety
about the timing of the commemoration. I thin k it is important that she works hard to
get them on board with this.
10 Mar 2011 Canterbury Earthquake Commemoration Day Bill 17149
I did not think I ever would have felt suppo rtive of “red and black”. I am a strong
Wellingtonian, and when it comes to it, at least as far as New Zealand is concerned, in
the National Provincial Championship I support Wellington, and anyone who is playing
Canterbury. We have seen the fervour of some of us watching the rugby match last
Friday night. I send our best wishes to the Crusaders, and if they can do the London
thing I think that would be a wonderful opportunity for the tens—or hundreds—of
thousands of New Zealanders in Europe. If  they have an opport unity to be brought
together on that sort of occasion, I think that would be superb. It is an opportunity to get
together and remember, but it is also related to an event that shows some of the best of
Canterbury. Although I do not always want the Crusaders to win, I acknowledge the
fact that they regularly do. I certainly hope they will on that occasion.
I do not know whether the Minister in charge of the bill has given a briefing in this
area yet, but it might be an opportunity for he r to give some further explanation around
the international fund th at Mr Weldon has been engaged to  work on for the next 4 to 6
weeks. Getting the pitch of it right is very important. We cannot be seen to be in a
situation like Haiti. We are not. We are not a poor country, and we have to be very, very
careful not to be seen to be begging for others to do what is our responsibility to put
right. I understand that a figure of $2 billion has been set by  the Prime Minister as the
objective of the fund. I think we need to be very clear right from the outset about the use
of that money. In my opinion, it should be used for extra things—not to replace things,
but used for things that were not there befo re—in order to make Christchurch a better
and more attractive place.
Like many of us in the last couple of weeks,  with Parliament not sitting, I have had a
little bit of time on my hands. I have had a look at the articles about Kobe and what
happened there. It was a double disaster. There was an earthquake, and then, effectively,
there was an abandonment of the city by some of its leadership and some of the city’s
most important people. As a result, Kobe has effectively become a low-income refuge. I
was discussing that situation this morni ng with one of the leading young brains of
Canterbury, whose name is not unfamiliar to this place. James Caygill said he was
confident that that situation would not happen in Canterbury and that there are people of
his generation and younger who are so firmly Cantabrians that they will stay.
However, I just want to signal that I think there is a danger that people are scared and
that as a result they might stay away, and th ere is also the possibility that many of the
opportunities that people need mi ght not now be available in  Christchurch. So as we
rebuild Christchurch we have to think of ways of  rebuilding the city’s people strength.
Some of my initial thoughts for the Minister would invol ve some very well-endowed
chairs at the university so that some of the best professors from around the world could
be attracted to Canterbury, for ei ther a shorter term or a long er term, in order to rebuild
the university. A similar approach could be taken to PhD scholarships so that we can get
people to come to Christchurch, even if it is for only 4 or 5 years.
I am glad Mr Joyce has returned to th e Chamber, because I am working on the
assumption that he has responsib ility for internati onal education. I gi ve him one little
piece of advice. A couple of tim es in the past, after crises  with international students—
and this has not been very public—we have found it very worthwhile to send a Minister
of Education to China quite early in the pr ocess in order to give some explanations
there. Those in both China and Japan have v
ery much appreciated that. I think in the
interests of longer-term relations hips that if we are seen to  be sending senior personnel
there, even if for only a day, to meet with officials and with whichever family members
can be gathered there, it would be very mu ch appreciated. Not only do we have to look
after our own commemorations, but we have  to acknowledge that a significant
17150 Canterbury Earthquake Commemoration Day Bill 10 Mar 2011
proportion of the people who have died are no t from New Zealand. We need to ensure
that that is acknowledged and that those relationships are maintained.

items.speaker: ALLAN PEACHEY
items.text: Thank you, Mr Deputy Speaker, for the
opportunity to make a few comments on the second reading of the Canterbury
Earthquake Commemoration Day Bill. I will take a moment to reflect on the 6 years I
had in Christchurch in the later years of the 1960s and the early 1970s as a student of
Canterbury University—in particular, and most fortuitous ly, as a student of what was
known as the town site, those beautiful build ings to which I always used to return
whenever I was in the centre of Christchurch to take a moment’s rest on the seats in the
old courtyard where we used to gather as students and enjoy the beauty of the city.
I take a moment to reflect also on the 60-plus years of my life and on the small and
larger tragedies that from time to time have befallen the people of this country—the
most poignant for me being the Tangiwai di saster in 1953. As it was with those
tragedies, so it has been, and so it will be, with Christchurch, with the rescue of the
trapped, the rescue and treatme nt of the injured, the recovery and mourning of the lost,
and the reflection on the power of nature but also on the po wer of human love and the
spirit, which we all have, that can never ever be beaten. As those qualities were brought
to other tragedies, so they are being brought, and will continue to be brought, to
Christchurch and Canterbury. The lives of th e people who are affected will be rebuilt,
and the city will also be rebuilt. Thank you.

items.speaker: Hon MARYAN STREET
items.text: First of all, I will  begin by recognising and
paying tribute to those who lost their lives in the 22 February earthquake in Canterbury.
I think of their loved ones and the people who are grieving for them. I also wish to
acknowledge those who have been injured and who are still suffering and trying to
recover from serious injury. For some, the me ntal injury will be the difficult issue to
deal with and will linger for a long time.
Just a few minutes ago on my BlackBerry I received a photo. It was a photo of the
United States - New Zealand Partnership Fo rum, of which I was a part. The photo was
taken at the AMI Stadium about  an hour before the earthqua ke struck. It was a forum
that consisted of some very high-powered US delegates. Fortunately those on the largest
congressional visit to this coun try that there had ev er been had left ea rlier that morning
for Wellington, so were out of harm’s way. However, Kurt Campbell, the Assistant
Secretary of State for East Asian and Paci fic Affairs, Christopher Hill, the previous
Assistant Secretary of State for East As ian and Pacific Affairs, numerous business
leaders from the United States, corporate dign itaries, an only recently retired senator,
and their wives and partners were all assemb led with their New Zealand counterparts. It
is good to have this lovely picture taken ac ross the breadth of the AMI Stadium at that
time.
By the time the earthquake struck, the conference had divided up into small groups to
go out and visit and have lunc h briefings with Christchurch businesses. I was at Tait
Electronics, out towards the airport; others  were dispersed around the city. It was a
circumstance that gave the American ambassa dor, as he said to me later, 2 hours of
panic as he tried to assemble all his comp atriots from around the c ity. I pay tribute to
the Defence Force personnel and the staff at the Antarctic Centre where, by about 4.30
p.m
., we had all assembled, mostly in on e piece. People had been evacuated from
around the city and assembled together by the good offices of the American Embassy,
the Ministry of Foreign Affairs and Trade, and every remotely official person who was
connected with the United States - New Z ealand Partnership Forum. Stephen Jacobi,
who leads that forum, deserves particular  mention for his professionalism and his
concern and care for our United States guests. At 12.51 p.m. we had just finished having
a briefing at Tait Radio Communications, part of Tait Electronics. We had just been told
10 Mar 2011 Canterbury Earthquake Commemoration Day Bill 17151
that we were in one of the safest possible buildings, a round, singl e-storey building, and
so it proved to be.
The earthquake struck with a bang, which I am not used to. Comi ng from Taranaki I
am used to hearing earthquakes before they arrive, or feeling them as little shudders
building into a larger one. Bu t this explosion took us all completely by surprise. The
ferocity of the shudder, the sideways move ment, was truly frightening. Then the power
went out and the lights went off and the 10 or so of us w ho were around that lunch table
dived under the table, with glassware and crockery flying and smashing around us.
When the power came on, through  the back-up system that Tait had, we all went
outside. The staff had been evacuated outsi de. Then the phone calls started and the
stories started to come back immediately. In  particular, I remember two sentences from
a woman who worked for Tait who was standing just a couple of metres away from me.
She was obviously phoning in to a loved one in  the central city. She was saying: “Gosh,
that was big, wasn’t it?”, when suddenly her face changed and she started repeating for
those of us around her what she was heari ng. The two sentences I recall most vividly
were: “The cathedral’s down. There are dead people.”
Suddenly the enormity of it began to strike  us. As we evacuated I took a couple of
American guests under my wing. They were very shocked by this event, but I took them
to the airport, which by that stage had been  evacuated. We took refuge in the Sudima
Hotel. After a short time the American Emba ssy got messages through to its delegates,
saying: “If you are near to th e Antarctic Centre, go there.” Of course, the Antarctic
Centre is a matter of metres away from th e Sudima Hotel, out by the airport, so we
walked to the Antarctic Centre. That building was not in  terribly good nick either—bits
of ceiling had fallen in—but it was better than  many others. By 8 o’clock that night all
of the American guests and many of the New Zealanders present at the United States -
New Zealand Partnership Forum had been evacuated by Hercules to Wellington, feeling
very lucky to get out so quickly. So to those Defence Force personnel and to the
officials who rallied every available service, I pay a tribute. I also pay a tribute to the
Christchurch-based members in this House, from all sides, who have been working with
their people, alongside their peopl e, assisting them in their gr ief and in the catastrophic
disruption of their lives. Those members ha ve our support, and if there is anything
practical we can do—if staying away is the best thing we can do—then they need only
to let us know.
I will make another comment about the memorial day. I want to reflect on two
cultures that are not my own: one is M āori and the other is Jewish. Both of them have
something in common. They both wait a year af ter an event, after a bereavement. They
wait a year, and then they return to the place and unveil a headst one. I cannot help
thinking, with all the reverence I can muster for the people of Chri stchurch, that this
memorial day is too soon. A year from now, when people are learning to live with their
grief—the grief that they cannot see a way through at the moment—they can return to
the place and we can grieve collectively.
Immediately after I returned to Wellington I had to go to China for an official visit
that had already been scheduled. At every formal meeting I attended in China people
began with a tribute to New Zealand and th e expression of their condolences for the
earthquake victims and the suffering that pe ople were enduring in New Zealand. I in
return was able to thank them for that an d express our condolences  for those Chinese
students who perished in the CTV building co llapse. In addition, I was able to thank
them for President Hu Jintao’s very gene rous financial contri bution of US$500,000 to
New Zealand. In addition to that, I thanked them for their immediate dispatching of
search and rescue teams to a ssist us. They know what it is  like. I visited the Tangshan
earthquake memorial. They have a dignified memorial there to 240,000 people who lost
17152 Canterbury Earthquake Commemoration Day Bill 10 Mar 2011
their lives in 1976. They know what it is li ke. Around the world, regardless of numbers
or scale, grief and loss are the same. Kia ora koutou.

items.speaker: KEITH LOCKE
items.text: I think this debate—it is hard to call it a debate, because
everyone is going in the same direction—has sh own that we all have a connection with
Christchurch. The earthquake was not just a Christchurch event; it was one that has
affected just about everyone in New Zeala nd, and I think that has come out in today’s
speeches. Maryan Street’s speech just before  was about being in Christchurch, Charles
Chauvel’s speech was about relations in Chri stchurch, and Allan Peachey’s speech was
about the time he spent in Christchurch. I think everyone is connected in some way with
friends or relations in that city. That is w hy it is such a difficult and emotional issue for
us.
I spent the first 22 years of my life in Christchurch and have relations there who have
suffered in the earthquake—a sister and a sister-in-law, in particular, as well as a
brother-in-law and family. There is also physical damage, which is why the debate
around heritage and what will be  reconstructed is so importa nt. To a significant extent,
the identity of the city is related to the buildings and to the built nature of the city.
There is also the environment to consider. I was brought up next to the Avon River,
in what is now known as the Avon Loop. I went back there a week ago, and the
riverbank I used to play on is now much wider as a result of the lateral spread. The river
has come up, the river has narrowed, and there are big, metre-wide cracks, etc., and that
makes one feel very sad. No doubt we will get over that; it is more the effect on the
people that we are most worried about.
Just to give members a feeling of the eff ect on people, I thought I would read a piece
from a friend of mine, Pam Vickers, who lives on Clifton Hill, next to Sumner. Her
experience is very well put: “The gossip round the water cooler at the office has been
exchanged for gossip at the water tanker, as  we queue up with our plastic bottles for
what we are most short of—water. Who has le ft town with who? Who is sleeping in a
tent? Who is sleeping in the garage? Few people here—along with Lyttelton, the worst
affected part of the city—want to sleep in the house, if they can avoid it.
Water is heavy and I haven’t quite got the knack of balancing it on my head, but I am
certainly adept at carrying three very large water bottles—one in each hand and the third
in between, supported by both sets of fingertip s. Everything looks grey, the colour of
the liquefied earth squeezed out of the ground like toothpaste by the earthquake. It has
been shovelled into piles by our fantastic stud ent army, but it has dried in the heat and
the dust is picked up and blown around by th e strong north-wester ly winds, covering
everything. The fruit on the tr ees no longer has an autumnal  ripeness, but is also the
colour of grey. This greyness is punctua ted by the odd moment of colourful humour—
usually about the way we are getting rid of human waste. Drains and sewers are broken,
so gardens are invaluable now.
And the aftershocks keep coming. Someone in  England asked me, ‘Do they feel like
little electric shocks?’  No they damn well do not. Th ey are small earthquakes that
follow the big one. They throw our stomachs into our throats and in a split second I am
taken back to where I was when the big one hit—the cathedral cafe, ground zero for all
of the destruction. I felt it coming and scr eamed to everyone there to get down. The
events from there are still too cruel and too raw to talk about. The aftershocks still shake
rubble from our homes and have a noise a nd movement under our feet that confirm
there is no such thing as terra firma.
Our nerves are frayed, our sleep disrupt ed, our tempers frazzled, and we live on a
diet of all-day earthquake news and anothe r tin of cold food … Thank goodness we had
the rehearsal with the 4 September quake, otherwise I don’t think we would be doing as
well as we are. Did I really say th
at!
10 Mar 2011 Canterbury Earthquake Commemoration Day Bill 17153
This one was big, and it was as though we had been hit by an atomic bomb. With our
landmarks no longer there it was hard to recogn ise Sumner or Christchurch in the first
days after the earthquake. Is  this really our home? Go ing up our road, coming home
from the water tanker, we cross crevices in a domestic car that might challenge an all-
terrain vehicle. Road cones, danger tape a nd yellow paint mark the cracks, humps and
road edges where the cliff has fallen away. You need nerves of steel to navigate it all—
waiting for another aftershock to drop you into  a hole or dislodge a boulder to land on
your head. It’s like a war zone.
We find ourselves doing strange things. I stand in the middle of a room piled high
with debris and pick up a screw. I look at it for a long period wondering ‘What is this
off?’. It is as though in this heap of damaged possessions I will ever find where it
belongs. It is all headed for the dustbin. I ta lk to my neighbour, who says she has spent
10 minutes just looking at a butterfly when she should be tidying up. Life seems unreal
and time seems to unravel. We keep telling ourselves time will put this right. With time,
the aftershocks will lessen. With time, power and water and sewage will be restored.
With time, our roads will be repaired. With time our houses will be rebuilt. With time.
But at the moment time goes slowly. Time brings us pain and anguish—and fear that we
might not have the strength to get through this . Time brings despair because all that we
have built up has gone and our future is in jeopardy.”
That description was from Pam Vickers. Last night her power did come on, but she is
still without water and sewerage, as are many people in the city of Christchurch. There
is still a lot more to do to help people in the east of Christchurch. Teams are still going
door-to-door, helping people. The Green Party has a team going around most days, or
every day. Kennedy Graham is in Christchurch leading that work.
We have to remember, as we prepare for the memorial service, that the recovery will
require a combination of effort: voluntary effort, such as the students and farmers are
engaged in along with all kind s of other organisations, in cluding church organisations
and community organisations; the official response throug h civil defence in all its
various parts; and all of the citizens of Ch ristchurch, in their own particular way,
helping and working together. It will take a while to recover, but we cannot slacken our
efforts right now. Thank you.

items.speaker: MICHAEL WOODHOUSE
items.text: In my short call on the Canterbury
Earthquake Commemoration Day Bill I comme nd not only the many thousands of staff
and volunteers who are working in Christch urch and the surrounding areas, but also the
many thousands of people who have opened their hearts and their homes right around
the South Island, particularly in my own city of Dunedin. People there have adopted a
rather novel approach to pr oviding support by opening at th e Dunedin Railway Station
the “Christchurch Embassy”. It is probably th e first embassy for a city anywhere that I
can think of, but it is a terrifi c initiative that has brought to gether organisations such as
the Citizens Advice Bureaux, the Order of St John—

items.speaker: Hon Trevor Mallard
items.text: They used to have one at the Back Bencher.

items.speaker: MICHAEL WOODHOUSE
items.text: Well, there you go; it wa s pinched off the Back
Bencher, which is always a pioneer.
It has also given to those of us who we re not in Christchurch on 22 February, and
who simply cannot imagine what life has been like since then, a small insight into the
trauma that was created for those who have been effectively displaced, and who are now
being accommodated in our schools, homes, a nd workplaces. I commend the work that
they are doing.
The Octagon saw around 10,000 people stop for 2 minutes’ silence last week, and if
that is a measure of what the memorial will  be like, North Hagley Park will be a quite
special place next Friday. I do not agree with the member Maryan Street that this
17154 Canterbury Earthquake Commemoration Day Bill 10 Mar 2011
commemoration day is too early ; I think it is a necessary catharsis, and I certainly
support it.

items.speaker: DARIEN FENTON
items.text: I do not want to change the tone of the debate, at all,
because I think the contributions on the Canterbury Earthquake Commemoration Day
Bill have been very genuine and heartfelt. It has been very moving to hear the
contributions from all sides of the House, and particularly the stories that have been told
by people such as my colleague Maryan St reet, who was there when the earthquake
happened.
I am absolutely petrified of earthquakes. I am like Lianne Dalziel,  who said after the
September earthquake that she had always thought the place to be frightened was
Wellington. Of course, that is now not the case. I come from a place in the country,
Auckland, where we do not think we have earthquakes, but apparently we do. Chris
Hipkins showed me yesterday a little gadge t he has on his iPhone that records every
earthquake in the country, and there are masses of them all over the country. It was
amazing to see. I live in Auckland, as I sa id, and I think I am safe—apart from the
volcanoes, of course, but that is another matter.
As I said, I commend all of the speakers for their very moving contributions, and I
repeat my sympathy for all of those in Christchurch who are suffering because of loss of
life, loss of home, loss of jobs, and so on.
Just in case we do not get to have a very long debate in the Committee stage, I will
turn to the bill in this sec ond reading speech, if I may. It is a pretty straightforward bill,
and I think the Minister of Labour and the department have done a good job. It is a
pretty simple approach. The bill provid es for a one-off public holiday on 18 March—
that is, next Friday—in the Canterbury region to commemorate the Christchurch
earthquake, when there will be a commemoration service at Hagley Park.
I am just seeking information, because I am not sure of my information. I have
already had quite a few texts, calls, and emails—and I know that my colleagues in
Christchurch are getting these too—about wh at the day actually means. What does it
mean for workers? What does it mean for busin ess? It is a day that will be treated like
any other public holiday, except that it will apply only to Canterbury, which means that
employees can be required to work if their agreement says they can be required to work.
If employees work on all or part of the day, then they must be paid time and a half and
they are entitled to an alternative day off. At  the moment that alternative day off has to
be agreed; after 1 April if it cannot be agr eed the employer can decide when that day
will be. Of course, there is a reference to the Education Act, which means that schools
will be closed for the day, as well.
I will mention some of the issues that  are coming up; I know that the Minister
mentioned them in her first reading speech. For example, businesses are expressing
some concern about this bill. I was just talk ing to my colleague Lianne Dalziel, who is
in Bexley, and she expressed concern—as, indeed, have other members in Christchurch.
Some shops in Bexley, where she works, have opened today for the first time. It is the
first time people have been able to get into their premises, and they are really concerned
about having to provide for time and a half or  a day off next Friday. I know that other
employers are complaining about having to fund a public holiday. It is not that they are
against it; it is just that some of them are so much on the margins that they say it could
tip them over.
There are a whole lot of ot her issues, as well. Somebody earlier in the discussion
referred to the workers who had been transfe rred into Christchurch to help out, and who
have now been transferre d out—people who are living an d working in Timaru, for
example, or people who have been transfer red to other parts of the country by their
employers, who have other places in New Z ealand where they can work. Will they be
10 Mar 2011 Canterbury Earthquake Commemoration Day Bill 17155
entitled to a public holiday? You know, there are issues, and there will be questions
about those people that will need to be addressed.
Of course, there are some real difficulties concerning other questions that are coming
up. Businesses are asking whether they are sup posed to close, and I think the Minister
needs to make that clear. Because it is  a commemoration day, some businesses do not
understand that they do not have  to close. They have to le t their staff off on pay, or pay
them time and a half. Because it is a co mmemoration day it feels something like Anzac
Day, when there is no trading. But there is trading, under this bill. I think that needs to
be made clear.
Another question that has come up is about the situation if sta ff want to only go to
the commemoration service and do not want to take the day off. What are they entitled
to? How does that work? A very practical  question came, once again, from Lianne
Dalziel, who is dealing in Bexley with c onstituents who still do not have access to
Portaloos or chemical toilets. She asks where the Portaloos will come from if thousands
of people pour into Hagley Pa rk. I am not being facetious he re; that is a very practical
question that I think needs to be given some  consideration. That is why many members
on our side of the House are sa ying that it is ju st too soon, and we are not sure whether
these practical considerations have been thought through.
Then we have all the workers who, of c ourse, do not have jobs. I mentioned in my
previous speech that millions of dollars have been paid out to employers to cover staff
and individual employees. But another categor y of employees cannot even get to their
jobs, because of their personal situations—for example, they have no toilets or showers,
no transport, or their children are off school. Their employers are saying that their jobs
are available, and because their jobs are availa ble they are not entitled to any subsidies.
Those people are at home without any income.
Then there is a whole other category of  workers who are in no man’s land: their
workplaces are still up and running, but orde rs have reduced by 80 percent. So the
laying off of staff has begun, but they are no t entitled to a subsidy situation. There are
other stories, as well, that I think will need some answers.
The other thing I will raise for the Minister—it may not be the time; it is not related
so much to this bill—is that there ar e workers who are employed by multinational
companies, international companies, which I understand are not eligible for earthquake
cover. Hundreds of cleaners in  the central business district , for example, are getting no
support at all at the moment.
There are issues but, as we have said all along, Labour will support this bill. We
support the people of Christchur ch, and we will join in comi ng together to grieve next
Friday.

items.speaker: NIKKI KAYE
items.text: I will start by paying tribute to the
New Zealand men, women, and children who lo st their lives on 22 February. I also pay
tribute to the overseas citizens who lost their lives. I think many of us would
acknowledge that the earthquake has been a pr etty horrific tragedy for this country, and
many New Zealanders might not have lost someone but will know of someone who has
been lost. But in such a time of tragedy we have also seen some extraordinary New
Zealanders step up. To mention just a few, I know that so many New Zealanders around
the country have offered anything from a bed to some linen and some food. I
acknowledge all of those New Zealanders who have stepped up.
We have also seen some extraordinar y leadership come through. The Student
Volunteer Army has captured the respect of th e nation. I think those students have also
captured the pride of the nation. One of the thin gs about this crisis is that sometimes it
takes an extraordinary crisis to change the va lues of a nation. That is one of the positive
things that could come from this.
17156 Canterbury Earthquake Commemoration Day Bill 10 Mar 2011
Everybody has a story. A lady walked into  my office recently who had not known
that her husband was travelling to Christch urch on the day of the earthquake. He was
actually working in the Pyne Gould building. Fortunately for her—and for him—he had
popped out for a coffee. So that day he lived, but he was one of the lucky ones. Her
story is not unique; many pe ople around New Zealand are shar ing those stories, and I
think that is a really important part of the process.
Finally, I pay tribute to the New Zealand armed forces. I had the opportunity, with
our Minister of Defence, to be on board HMNZS Canterbury and to see the
extraordinary support that our New Zealand ar med forces were giving to the people of
Canterbury. It really made me reflect, as I hope many other members of Parliament will
do, on the huge contribution that our armed fo rces are making in Canterbury at this
time.
I am very pleased to support the Canter bury Earthquake Commemoration Day Bill. I
acknowledge that even though there has been  an extraordinary tragedy, so many New
Zealanders around the country are stepping up in every possible way, and that is making
a huge difference to the lives of so many Ne w Zealanders, particul arly the people of
Canterbury.

items.speaker: CHARLES CHAUVEL
items.text: I begin my short cont ribution in the second
reading debate of the Canterbury Earthquake Commemoration Day Bill by
acknowledging the Minister of Labour for addressing in her second reading speech
some potential concerns I raised in my firs t reading speech. I accept that the choice of
timing is never easy, and that there are always pros and cons.
I agree with Trevor Mallard that a decision has been settled on, and the course of
action, which is the commemoration on 18 Ma rch, is now clear. It does leave a further
decision, which is what opportunity  there will be at a later da te for the entire nation to
have an opportunity to mourn, to commemorate, and to cel ebrate what we know will be
the recovery of Canterbury. Maybe the idea advanced by Maryan Street about an
unveiling in a year’s time from the anniversary of the earthquake is an appropriate thing
to consider.
I mentioned in my initial contribution the services that were held around the nation
on the first day of this month. I think they reveal a real need amongst New Zealanders
outside Canterbury to participate in that process. I will say no more on the issue other
than to respectfully urge the Minister and her colleagues to consider that need, because I
do think it is real. As I sa id, Labour accepts the decision with regard to the timing and
the regional nature of the holiday we are discussing now. But I think it is very important
that we acknowledge that wider need, and acknowledge the importance of making sure
everybody has an opportunity to, as I said, enga ge in that three-stage process: mourn
those whom we have lost, co mmemorate the event, then look forward to the future. I
hope looking forward to the future is something we can all begin to focus on.
I really encourage Ministers and members of the Government to think about two
things as we move forward. One is the need  for compassion. We have heard all sorts of
comments in the last couple of weeks about looters. Many would say fair enough; that
sort of behaviour is terrible. But let us not forget that th ere is other be haviour going on
such as profiteering, price gouging, and excessive renting. We need to think about the
people who are affected by that sort of beha viour. As far as I am concerned it is every
bit as bad as looting. We may need to thi nk about taking powers, as has been done in
the United States in post-emergency situati ons, that provide some ability in the short
term to control that sort of activity. We may need to do that so that people, particularly
those at the bottom and in the middle, who need  to rent commercial premises or houses
and need to buy goods and serv ices are not affected by th e rawness of the rules of
supply and dem
and. That is the first hope I express going forward.
10 Mar 2011 Canterbury Earthquake Commemoration Day Bill 17157
The second one is to urge the Governme nt to be far-sighted. There is a huge
opportunity here for the people of Christchurch and Canterbury when it comes to
rebuilding what has been lost. Would it not be fantastic to see a true eco-city, with
businesses and houses built to the highest en ergy-efficiency standards, a world-class
transport system, and clever town planning,  while preserving the beautiful heritage
buildings wherever possible? We shoul d concentrate on the intellectual and
entrepreneurial opportunities that the city has going forward, such as the wonderful
cleantech sector; the university, which is a real jewel in the crown; the tourism
businesses that contribute so many jobs ; and the other educational and training
institutions. There is a huge  opportunity to get people upsk illed and to address all the
training needs that we know people have, so th at they can go forward and contribute to
the rebuilding of the city.
It would be fantastic if, rather than looking inward and being preoccupied with the
awful past we have all spoken about today, we were able to look forward with pride and
have a think about the opportunities that that sort of visionary rebuild would guarantee
to that magnificent city in the South Island. With those words I commend the bill to the
House in the second reading.

items.speaker: COLIN KING
items.text: One cannot avoid the tragedy of what
happened in Christchurch on 22 February 2011  at 12.51 p.m. We are now at the second
reading stage of the Canterbury Earthquake Commemoration Day Bill, and I think it is
quite appropriate that the interpretation clause makes specific reference to the
Christchurch Show Day. Notwithstanding all the tragedy, loss, grief, and dislocation
that have happened in that community, that  in itself conjures up the thought of the
country and the town coming t ogether and celebrating the un ity that we have all grown
to have amazing confidence in. When I was a child the highest structure in Christchurch
was the cathedral, and on the odd day when one was up on the Port Hills and looked
across at a canopy of fog, the only thing sticking out would be the cathedral. It will take
a lot of work for us to ensure that our ch ildren and our grandch ildren have a similar
view to us as children of Christchurch as a city of excitement and flair and colour.
I will move on to one aspect of the event in  North Canterbury. It is interesting that a
lot of families still send their children to the various colleges of eminence in
Christchurch, and it is pleasing to see th at the community of North Canterbury,
especially the area schools—and I will me ntion them; they are Amuri Area School,
Hurunui College, and Cheviot Area School—were able to open their doors for whatever
time will be necessary to children who have been displaced from those colleges.
We look forward to 18 March, when we w ill come together to support one another
and to look toward a brighter future. I am aware that the speakers that have gone before
have very eloquently articulated the heartfel t emotion of it all. Leaving it at that, I
commend this bill to the House.
Bill read a second time.
Procedure

items.speaker: CHRIS TREMAIN
items.text: I seek leave of the House to go to
the third reading of the Ca nterbury Earthquake Commemoration Day Bill forthwith and
to forgo the Committee stage.

items.speaker: The ASSISTANT SPEAKER
items.text: Leave is sought for that purpose. Is there
anyone opposed to that course of action? It appears not. Leave is granted.
17158 Canterbury Earthquake Commemoration Day Bill 10 Mar 2011
Third Reading

items.speaker: Hon KATE WILKINSON
items.text: I move, That the Canterbury
Earthquake Commemoration Day Bill be now read a third time . As we have heard from
other speakers in the House today, the Christchurch earthquake will shape the identity
of the Canterbury region for many years to come, and I appreciate the positive
contributions of other speakers so far. I think there is a wonderful opportunity for
Canterbury to rebuild. After hearing the contribution from some of the Wellington
speakers, I have to say that  if the Crusaders get too good the Hurricanes might not be
able to beat them in the near future, but we certainly appreciate the gesture. I also
appreciate that there was mutual agreement that the game that was due to be played be a
draw.
On a more serious note, this bill provide s for Friday, 18 March to be the day of
commemoration to mark the tragedy that we have all suffered and the devastating
consequences that it has brought. The death to ll of this day is yet to be officially
confirmed, but we know that some 200 families may have lost a loved one. Those of us
from Canterbury all have a link to someone who has died, whether it is a personal
friend, a colleague, or a passi ng acquaintance whom we happened to meet. In some
respects, though, the entire nation is grieving. Th e grief is, of course, most real for the
people of Canterbury, but, none the less, I be lieve that the entire nation is grieving, and
I certainly thank people for that.
Tens of thousands of people have damaged homes and property. Many of those need
to be rebuilt entirely. The entire region is exhausted by the continuing aftershocks. Our
nerves are always on edge, and it is important that the region is provided with an
opportunity to come together to grieve as a community. The memorial to take place next
Friday will be a day of mour ning. It will be a difficult day for many of us, but I believe
that it is crucial. I know that there are so me genuine concerns about the cost to some
businesses, and this is the case for all public  holidays. But sometimes in the context of
an extraordinary tragedy we need to look pa st these short-term costs and focus on what
we believe will help the people of Canterbury as a whole at this time. I believe that
allowing this day to be observed as a public ho liday is the best way to ensure that all
Cantabrians have the opportunity  to attend the memorial at Ha gley Park, to take a step
back from the carnage for a moment, and to grieve.
I once again thank the members of this House for the concern, the compassion, and
the support for Canterbury and for Christch urch during these tr agic times. I again
commend the bill to the House.

items.speaker: Hon TREVOR MALLARD
items.text: The Opposition parties will,
of course, be supporting the third read ing of the Canterbury Earthquake
Commemoration Day Bill.
I will start off by doing something that maybe  I should have done ea rlier, and that is
to acknowledge and thank the Canterbury MPs, and in particular the Christchurch MPs,
for the work they are doing th ere. I have been lucky enough to hear from their—I was
going to say “emissary”, but Mr Cosgrove  is not normally regarded as having
diplomatic status. He has come out of Canterbury a couple of times when the others
have not in order to brief colleagues on th e situation. It has become clear that an
enormous amount of work is going on there,  even though the personal circumstances of
the MPs are not a lot different from the pe rsonal circumstances of many of those who
have been affected. We know of colleagues sl eeping in tents in the backyard. We know
that all of them are doing enormous work, an d that a couple of them have lost their
houses. It is a truly awful situation, but, like Kiwis do, they are putting their all into it.
10 Mar 2011 Canterbury Earthquake Commemoration Day Bill 17159
I acknowledge that in a way this tragedy is developing a sense of community, and it
is a community that occurs within the city and within th e country, and that has been
exemplified by this debate here today. Like all families and all communities, some of us
might have done things in a slightly different way, but now that we know that a decision
has been made for this approach to be taken, we will get in behind it and make sure that
the commemoration is the best that it can possibly be.
One of the things I am hoping is that out of this tragedy, acro ss the country and in
this Parliament—I am an optimist, but I am not unrealistic; we cannot be like this all the
time—we will learn that there are strength s all around the House, and that the more
often that we can avail ourselves of those strengths, the bigger the contribution that
Parliament can make to the country. Having said that, I want to single out—and there
are always dangers in doing this—both the Minister for Canterbury Earthquake
Recovery and Mr Flavell for their contributions, and, but not  quite to the same extent,
Mr Locke as well. Things have been said from a Christchurch perspective by both the
Minister and Mr Locke that are very special, and Mr Flavell is someone who I think
exemplifies New Zealand’s understanding of deat h and has an ability to express it in a
way that many of us would love to be able to do.
I will share with the House the fact that  I spent a couple of minutes, 10 minutes ago,
with the senior Government whip and the Minister. I think we came to the conclusion
that in a legal sense this legislation is  unnecessary. The regulation-making powers that
we granted to the Government under the Act passed last year following the September
earthquake gave it the ability to create this  day. But we came to the conclusion together
that we as a Parliament are pleased that the powers that sat there are not being used, and
that there is an opportunity for members to  come together as a Parliament to be
supportive and to indicate agai n the fact that we care deeply for the people of
Christchurch and the people internationally who have lost people, for the people, young
and old, who do not know where they are go ing to live over the next few months and
over the next few years, and for the people who have been living, and are living, in what
are currently unacceptable circumstances.
What we have done is to resolve to do togeth er what we can to make the best of this
tragedy, to learn from it, but, most of all, to put on the record our commitment to make
sure that Canterbury is strong again, not only in the Crusaders sense but as an important
counterbalance to Auckland in a way that is important to our society and to our
economy. As we all know, although I love Dunedin, Canter bury is effectively the
capital of the South Island, and for New Zealand to be strong it must be strong too.

items.speaker: Hon HEKIA PARATA
items.text: T ēnā koe e te Mana
Whakawā, otira, ki a tātou o te Whare Pāremata. Tēnei te poroporoaki ki ngā tāngata, ki
ngā wh ānau o Ōtau tahi, o t āwāhi hoki. E ai ki tē tahi o ng ā rārangi i roto i te haka
taparahi, arā, ko t ēnei: “Ko R ūaumoko e ngunguru nei, au, au, au ē hā!”. I runga an ō i
tērā kōrero, kei te mōhio tātou ka rongo tonu tātou katoa i te mamae o ngā tāngata o tērā
wāhi o Ōtautahi. Nā reira, he poroporoaki poto noa iho i tēnei wā ki a rātou kua hipa atu
i te p ō, haere, haere, haere atu r ā. Hoki mai ki a t ātou te hunga ora, t ēnā koutou, t ēnā
koutou, tēnā koutou katoa.
[Greetings to you, Mr Assistant Speaker, and indeed to us of the House. This farewell
tribute is to the people and families of Chri stchurch, and to those from overseas, as
well. In the ceremonial haka, there is a line that goes like this: “It is I, R ūaumoko, the
earthquake god, rumbling here; take care, look out, be warned!”. On the basis of that
statement, we know that we will all continue to experience the pain of the people of that
place, Christchurch. So this brief farewell gesture at this mome nt to those who have
passed on into the void : farewell, depart, and journey on. I come back to us, the living:
greetings to you, greetings to you, and greetings to you all.]
17160 Canterbury Earthquake Commemoration Day Bill 10 Mar 2011
I join with every member of this House and with all New Zealanders in expressing
our sadness for those families here in Aotear oa New Zealand who have lost loved ones,
and those families who face the tragedy of havi ng either to come to New Zealand or to
wait in their home countries to receive back members of their families. We
acknowledge that the pain that has been e xperienced by everyone will take much longer
to go away than the days we have experienced so far, and, indeed, will last beyond the
commemorative day next Friday that the Canterbury Earthquake Commemoration Day
Bill puts in place. But part of the process is that we have the opportunity to come
together formally as a nation to recognise the grief, sadness, and loss in Canterbury, and
to begin the healing that will be part of the restoration and recovery of Christchurch and
the strengthening of communities in and around Canterbury, Te Wai Pounamu, and
New Zealand.
I went to Christchurch last week and had the opportunity to visit ethnic communities,
who were responding with the sa me resilience that has characterised the entire response
of Cantabrians to this tr agedy. Those communities wher e English is not the first
language were coping with their own particular  and special challenges. In situations of
stress, understanding the different cultural cues  of a different culture provides another
layer of complexity to the way that thos e communities can respond. Nevertheless, they
were binding together, sharing resources  amongst and between themselves, taking
