succour in their own cultural and religious practices, and gaining access to the services
that are available to all New Zealanders.
I had the opportunity also to visit the wo men’s refuges and to see again the strong
work that that group of wome n does both in normal times and in abnormal times. They
responded, as did everyone else , to the needs of their particular communities, and they
will continue to require support. One of the by-products of stress is sometimes violence
towards those closest to us. In recognising that that happens it  is important to
acknowledge that it is no more acceptable in tim es of tragedy than it is at any other
time. We must continue to provide support to organisations like Women’s Refuge to
meet the demands of the situation.
I also had the opportunity to visit Orion, the company responsible for getting
electricity back up throughout Christch urch. Its own building was rendered
uninhabitable by the earthquake. It operated from a marquee under an oak tree, and
subsequently in prefabricated buildings that had been trucked in to allow it to work to
get the electricity network up and going again. I pay tribute to those workers; as has
been remarked on by other speakers, many, ma ny of the workers, whoever they were—
whether working on restoring power lines or water, or for the Red Cross or the
Salvation Army—were themselves directly affected by the earthquake. Despite that,
they went out and provided the work that  was needed to begin the restoration and
recovery of Christchurch.
Finally, I mention the volunteers. They have  been an example to all of us of how
well New Zealanders respond to the needs of their neighbours and to the needs of
communities. Volunteers who live close to Christchurch and others who have travelled
from other parts of New Zealand have gone there to help in this time of need. It is really
important that we maintain the spirit of Kiwi voluntarism. It is important that we
acknowledge the contribution th at has been made by those volunteers, and that will
continue to be made, and it is important that  we recognise that there will be an ongoing
need for volunteers in the weeks and months ahead of us.
I join with the rest of th is House in supporting the passa ge of this bill. Although it
may not be legally necessary, it gives us the opportunity to come together as a
parliamentary community to recognise and respect the need for us as a nation to stand,
10 Mar 2011 Canterbury Earthquake Commemoration Day Bill 17161
as our Prime Minister has said, shoulder to  shoulder with the people of Canterbury. I
commend this bill to the House.

items.speaker: KEITH LOCKE
items.text: The Green Party fully supports the Canterbury
Earthquake Commemoration Day Bill. I woul d like to comment on Trevor Mallard’s
view that perhaps this bill was not nece ssary and perhaps the provision of a public
holiday could have been implemented unde r the Canterbury Earthquake Response and
Recovery Act, which gives very significant powers to the Government to override most
bits of existing legislation. I think it is good that we are passing this bill rather than
using those executive powers, because those powers have been under some criticism in
the community and in the legal fraternity.
There is a fear that the Government, if it chooses, could use those powers in a way
that is not appropriate. That little fear popped up in some of the community debate
about Gerry Brownlee’s comments on herita ge buildings, whether or not those
comments were rightly interpreted. I think th ere is a fear, despite the crisis, of giving
too much power to the Government as opposed to Parliament. So it is good that we are
debating this bill and will pass it today.
The cooperative spirit involved in devel oping legislation, having a debate, and
working together across parties is the sort of  cooperative spirit that is superior to the
Government just going its own way. It refl ects the cooperative spirit that has been
generated so well amongst the people of Ch ristchurch, and, more broadly, across the
whole of New Zealand. Other sp eakers have mentioned the international response. The
response from Australia and from many other countries has been fantastic. It will be a
challenge for this Parliament and for the pe ople of New Zealand to try to keep hold of
the best of that cooperative spirit of helping each other, of neighbours helping
neighbours, and all the sorts of things that have been generated around this tragedy. We
want to hold on to that as much as possible.
It is also important to recognise—and some times if we are outside Christchurch we
do not quite recognise it fully—that there ar e three other areas wh ere the solutions are
much further off. We are seeing more zones open up in the central business district and
the four avenues area, and we are seeing the power going back on for most people. I pay
tribute to Orion for what its staff have done. At least from the outside it looks like a
fantastic effort. They have gone on, day after day, working for long hours, and they
have used very creative solutions to get the power on to just about all areas. A few areas
still do not have power, and those people are still suffering.
But as I said, there are three other three ot her areas where solutions are much further
off. One is the area of water and sewera ge. The Bromley sewage treatment plant is
stuffed. Christchurch relies on that to a signi ficant extent, so processing sewage is a big
problem. There are water-quality problems th roughout the city, not only in the affected
east. Those problems will not be resolved very quickly, so we have to be very
supportive and put in alterna tive facilities there—Portaloos  and everything else—and
also make sure that they are cleaned out. A huge area is affected, and even with the
Portaloos the situation is not very nice for the people concerned. So that will be a big
area of concern.
The other area where there is a bit of testiness is in relation to the speed at which the
fix-up will take place—that is, people fixing up their houses. Of course, there is the
whole question of replacing houses and which houses cannot be replaced. That is a very
difficult problem for many people, but for people across the eastern part of Christchurch
most buildings have some fix-up require d. Getting the insurance, getting the
tradespeople—all of that stuff—will take a long time, and we have to be very supportive
wherever we can. Parliament and the Government have to support creative solutions.
17162 Canterbury Earthquake Commemoration Day Bill 10 Mar 2011
Sometimes tradespeople do not  get on the job unless they  are guaranteed payment.
There is debate at the moment between  the Earthquake Commission, tradespeople and
homeowners about who is payi ng, how quickly, and all the re st of it. We want to do
what we can to make sure all of that is resolved as smoothly as possible.
The third problem that requires a lot of  support—counselling as well as financial
support—is the whole question of people who do not know how they will survive
financially. I have struck that question all over the place with friends and relations. They
have perhaps rented out a flat  and their tenants have disappe ared, their flat is damaged,
their home is damaged, their business is damage d, or they are well behind as a result of
their business being closed for a few weeks.  There are piles and piles of people who
have financial problems, and who do not quite see their way out of them.
The Government is, of course, providing in terim grants and things like that, which
are benefiting a lot of people, and the Red Cro ss is too, but there is a lot of work to be
done for quite a long period to assist people in that area. I think we have a considerable
role to play in making sure the mechanis ms are there and in supporting the volunteer
efforts. Often those efforts have happened because of the initiative of the organisations
and the people concerned, but I think the Gove rnment has a responsibility to foster and
support those volunteer initiatives. They are a part of the cooperation ethic that has
arisen in this crisis. They are usually, cost-effective solutions , as well. Although
volunteer efforts require a certain resource, they achieve a lot, as well.
With those few comments, the Green Party supports this bill.

items.speaker: TE URUROA FLAVELL
items.text: Kia ora, Mr Assistant
Speaker. Kua k ōrerohia te āhuatanga o te titiro o te Ao M āori ki tē nei parekura nui n ō
reira waiho tērā ki reira. Hoi anō ko tāku ko te kī atu, arā anō tētahi tangata, nō Waikato
te tangata nei, ko Tetaki Tairākena tōna ingoa. I whakanuia tana rā whānau e 60 inā tata
nei. Ki te nuinga, ko Wally k ē te ingoa, ki taku m ōhio ko ia t ētahi kaiako m ō te reo
Māori mō ngā tau e 25. He nanakia te tangata nei m ō te purei i te rakuraku, te k ītā, ka
mutu, ki te waiata
i ngā waiata ngahau i roto i t ētahi pēne. E ai ki ng ā kōrero i te taha o
te tangata nei a Steve Apirana. Ā te R ātapu e t ū mai nei, ko ia t ērā ka takoto i tōna
marae i Tauwhare, he marae t ēnei tata ki Morrinsville, ā, ko ia t ētahi o ng ā aitu ā ka
nehua ā kō ake nei. Nō reira ko te kaupapa nui, āe, me whakanui ko te hunga kua ngaro
i te tirohanga kanohi. Hoi anō, kore taea te karo i tērā āhuatanga.
He hararei te rā kei mua i te aroaro? E, k ō tāku e kī nei, e kāo. Ehara i te hararei. Ko
te hararei he wā whakatā, he wā okioki, he wā ki te mahi i ngā mahi i tua atu o te mahi o
te wā. He hararei t ēnei? Karekau. He w ā kia tuku i ngā  whakaaro ki te hunga e noho
pani nei, ka mutu, ki te tautoko i te hunga e tangi tonu ana, kia tuku i ngā whakaaro ki te
hunga kua ngaro. Me t ū pokohiwi ki te pokohiwi ki te  taha o te hunga e noho m
ai rā ki
reira, Pākehā mai, Māori mai, te hunga nō tāwāhi mai, manene mai, koi nā te mahi nui ā
ngā rā kei mua i te aroaro. N ō reira m ō te kaupapa, kore taea te whakah ē.
Whakawāteahia mai he rā, me kī, mō tērā o ngā takiwā. Ko tāku noa ake ko te kī, āe, kai
te tautoko ake te Pāti Māori i tēnei o ngā āhuatanga.
Ko tāku kia whai w āhi tātou ki te mihi ki te hunga, ng ā ringa raupā , ngā kaiāwhina,
ngā mea whakapau werawera m ō tērā o ng ā hapori, otir ā, m ō te motu; kaua o roto
Aotearoa nei engari, mō te hunga i hara m ai i tāwahi anō hoki. Ko ngā mea o Hapanihi,
te hunga o Ahitereiria, ng ā pirihimana i hara mai i Ahitereia ki te tautoko. Ng ā mea o
roto o Amerika i hara mai i tawhiti kia eke mai ki konei, tautoko mai ai i a tātou.
Ko tāku he mihi ki te hunga ope t ūao, arā, te voluntary army. Me mihi nui ki a r ātou
ka tika, ng ā wātene M āori o te motu, Salvation Army, te R ōpū Hāpai R ū Whenua i
Rangiora, Student Volunteer Army, Farmy Army, Red Cross, me ngā marae o te motu. I
whakawātea mai ng ā marae o te motu i ō rātou kūaha ki te hunga i noho raruraru nei,
arā, kai raro iho nei, kei Pipitea tētahi i whakatuwhera nei i ngā kūaha o tō rātou marae.
10 Mar 2011 Canterbury Earthquake Commemoration Day Bill 17163
Engari, me pēnei rawa te mihi nui, me k ī, ki a Ng āi Tahu. Ko Ngā i Tahu tērā e kaha
tonu nei ki te hāpai, ki te āwhina, ki te noho hai pou, hai tuarā mō te hunga e rongo nei i
te ngau o mamae, P ākehā mai, Māori mai. Kai Wigram k ē rātou i tēnei wā tonu nei, kai
a rātou te nama waea hai āwhina i te hunga e kimi k ōrero nei, e kimi āwhina nei mai i
ngā moutere o Te Moana-nui-a-Kiwa, me ētahi atu. N ō reira, ka nui te mihi ki a r ātou
me ngā pūtea ka tukuna ki te kai, ki te āwhina. Nō rātou te whakaaro nui ki te hāpai, me
kī, i ngā mea e noho mai ra r ā i Te Wai Pounamu. Ng ā Hau E Whā  Marae, ko ia t ētahi
kua whakatuwhera nei i tōna kūaha, me kī, ki Te Manatū Whakahiato Ora, ka mutu, kua
noho tērā hei w āhi hāpai i te whakaoranga o te tangata. Me mihi r ā ki Te Puni K ōkiri
m
e ngā non-governmental organisations, ngā rōpū āwhina Kāwanatanga.
Nā reira, ko taku ko te mihi ki ng ā iwi katoa o te motu i roto i a au, an ā, kua
whakatuwherahia ng ā kura kaupapa M āori i te k ūaha ki ng ā tamariki o roto o Ng āi
Tahu, kia haere ki roto i a au o Te Arawa.
Hai kupu kōrero whakamutunga māku, i te whakaaro ake au mō tētahi aituā nui i roto
i a au, anā ko te hū o Tarawera i te tau 1890. I t ērā wā, e ai kī ngā kōrero, e 150 o Ngāti
Rangitihi-Tūhourangi i mate. N ā, i whakaw ātea mai a Te Arawa i ng ā kākahu, i ng ā
whenua, i ng ā kai ki te hunga m ōrehu, an ā, kei reira tonu t ērā here ki roto o te
Whakarewarewa ko Ngā ti W āhiao, ki Ng āpuna ko Ng āti Hurunga, ki Waitangi ko
Tapuika, ki Matatā ko Ngāti Rangitihi, anā, kei reira ng ā u ri i tēnei wā, nā te whakaaro
nui o ngā wāhi nei o roto i a au o Te Arawa ki te hunga i raruraru i tērā o ngā rū nui. Kai
te pērā anō hoki i t ēnei wā tonu nei, kua whakatuwherahia te ng ākau ki te āwhina, ki te
tautoko i te hunga kua parekuratia nā runga i te āhuatanga o te rū nei.
Me mihi ki a Ngāti Porou, me kī, ngā whanaunga o te Hōnore Hekia Parata, ki te reo
irirangi i kohi moni ki te āwhina, ki te Pouaka Whakaata M āori mō Hyundai CODE i
tuku i a Glen Osborne r āua ko Reuben Wiki ki te waiata, ahakoa koretake r āua ki te
waiata, te k ōhanga reo o t ēnei takiw ā, Te K ōhanga Reo o Ng ā Mokopuna, me Te
Kōhanga Reo o Te Kaahui, me k ī, i mahi i te kapa haka i Lambton Quay i nanahi nei ki
taku mōhio, ki ng ā nēhi o roto i a au o Te Arawa, a Waikato-Tainui i tuku i w ā rātou
kaihanga whare ki tērā takiwā, m
e tētahi tangata tērā pea kāore anō koe kia rongo mō te
tangata nei Mr Assistant Speaker, a Henare O’Keefe. N ō roto o Heretaunga t ēnei
tangata. Ko t āna mahi he heri i āna m īhini tunu kai. Koi n ā te ingoa o tana kaupapa
Tunutunu. Kua heria ki reira ki te tunu kai mō te hapori.
Ka mutu, me waiho pe a ki reira engari, ar ā anō ngā marae; Takahanga ki Kaik ōura,
Tuahiwi Marae ki Kaiapoi, Te Aitara kihi Marae ki Te Tihi-o-Maru, r ātou katoa kua
āwhina mai. N ō reira, ko tāku he mihi nui, whakaharahara o te ng ākau, otirā, o te P āti
Māori me te Pāremata, taku kī atu ki a rātou katoa i kaha ki te tautoko i te hapori e tangi
nei, e auwē nei, me te tūmanako ia nā runga i te āhuatanga kua whakawāteahia mai tēnei
rā, me whakanui i te hunga kua ngaro, waiho rā tou kia moe, kia okioki. Kua ea te w āhi
ki a rā tou. Ko t ā tātou he tuku i te roimata me te h ūpē kia ea ai te āhuatanga o m ate.
Huri noa, kia ora tātou.
[Greetings, Mr Assistant Speaker. Mention has been made of the Māori World’s view
on the Christchurch earthquake, so I will not ta ke that further. Let me begin by talking
about a man from Waikato by the name of Tetaki Tair ākena. Recently he celebrated his
60th birthday. To most, he was plain Wally.  To my knowledge, for over 25 years he
taught the Māori language. He was very good at playing the guitar and was even in a
band, according to some, alongside Steve Apira na. This Sunday he will lie in state on
his marae at Tauwhare, close to  Morrinsville. He is one of  the ones who is about to be
buried. So, yes, the most important thing is to acknow ledge those who are lost from
sight. Death is something that cannot be avoided.
Is it a holiday that is ahead of us? I say it is not. A holiday is a time to rest and
recuperate, to catch up on things that one is  not able to do on a wo rking day. Is this a
17164 Canterbury Earthquake Commemoration Day Bill 10 Mar 2011
holiday? No. It is a time to give thought to  those who have suffered the loss of loved
ones, to offer help to those who are stil l grieving, and to grieve for those who have
passed away. We must stand shoulder to shoulde r with the people over there, be it non-
Māori, Māori, people from beyond our shores, or migrants. That is the most important
thing ahead of us. The principle cannot be faulted. Set aside a day for the people of that
region of ours. I simply say that the Māori Party supports this emphatically.
Personally, I believe that it is an opportunity  for us to acknowledge the rescue
workers, the helpers, the ones who have worked tirelessly fo r that one of our
communities, and indeed the nation—not just the ones from here in New Zealand, but
those from overseas as well, particularl y the rescue workers from Japan, the police
from Australia, and those all the way from th e United States of America, who came to
support us.
I particularly want to acknowledge all the voluntary organisations. It is most
appropriate that we thank them immensely—M āori wardens of the country, the
Salvation Army, the Rangiora Express, the Student Volunteer Army, the Farmy Army,
the Red Cross, and the marae of the country. The marae opened up their doors to those
with difficulties. Pipitea Marae just down the street along from us was one. It opened up
its doors.
But Ngāi Tahu must be accorded the greatest a ccolade. They were resolute in their
efforts to lift morale and provide assistance and be a pillar and backbone for those who
suffered hardship, whether they were non-M āori or Māori. They are currently set up at
Wigram airbase. They have a telephone number to assist those seeking information and
assistance relating to Pasifika people and other people. So a huge a ccolade is due to
them and the financial help they provided fo r food and assistance. Ng āi Tahu have
enormous foresight to help thos e living in the South Island. Ng ā Hau e Wh ā Marae is
one that has opened up its doors to the Mi nistry of Social Development, which has
become a recovery assistanc e centre. Thanks indeed to the Ministry of Mā ori
Development and the non-governmental organisations.
I acknowledge all the tribes of th e country that are part of me. M āori-medium
schools have opened their door s to children within Ng āi Tahu to go and stay within me
in Te Arawa.
To conclude this address, I recall a huge disaster that oc curred in my area. It was
the eruption of Tarawera in the year 1890. At that time, and according to the stories,
150 of Ng āti Rangitihi-Tūhourangi perished. Te Arawa made clothing, land, and food
available to the survivors, and that bond with Ng āti Wāhiao of W.hakarewarewa, Ngāti
Hurunga of Ngāpuna, Tapuika of Waitangi, and Ngāti Rangitihi of Matatā still remains.
The descend
ants are still there today, due to the great regard of these places within me
in Te Arawa for those who suffered that huge earthquake. We have a similar situation
again today, where the heart is opened up to assist and support those who have become
victims of this disaster.
I need to acknowledge Ng āti Porou; relatives of the Hon Hekia Parata; radio
stations that raised money to help; M āori Television, for Hyundai CODE, releasing
Glen Osborne and Reuben Wiki to sing, even if their efforts were not very flash; M āori-
medium schools and language nurseries of this locality, such as Te Kōhanga Reo o Ngā
Mokopuna and Te K ōhanga Reo o Te Kaahui, which performed cultural items on
Lambton Quay yesterday, as I was told; th e nurses from within me of Te Arawa;
Waikato-Tainui, who sent their carpenters to  that place; and a person whom you may
not know anything about, Mr Assistant Spea ker, Henare O’Keefe. This person is from
Hastings. He owns a mobile barbecue kitchen. Its name is Tunutunu. He has taken it
down there to barbecue food for the community.
10 Mar 2011 Canterbury Earthquake Commemoration Day Bill 17165
Perhaps I should stop there, but before I do I need to mention the marae: the one in
Kaikōura, the Takahanga Marae; the Tuahiwi Mara e in Kaiapoi; and the Te Aitarakihi
Marae at Timaru—all have offered help. I extend my immense and heartfelt accolade,
and that of the M āori Party and Parliament, as well,  to all those who supported the
community here, which is grieving and hurting so strongly, in the hope that this day will
be set aside. Celebrate those who have perish ed. Allow them to sleep and rest. The part
concerning them has been fulfilled. Ours is  to shed tears and mucus, to acquit our
losses through death. Thank you to all of us, throughout the Chamber.]
Bill read a third time.

10 Mar 2011 Business Statement 17117 
THURSDAY, 10 MARCH 2011 
Mr Speaker took the Chair at 2 p.m. 
Prayers. 
BUSINESS STATEMENT 
Hon SIMON POWER (Acting Leader of the House): Next week it is the 
Government’s intention to make furthe r progress on the Marine and Coastal Area 
(Takutai Moana) Bill. 
Hon TREVOR MALLARD (Labour—Hutt South) : Can I seek from the Acting 
Leader of the House an undertaking that there is a continuanc e of the previous 
undertaking not to take that bill under urgency. 
Hon SIMON POWER (Acting Leader of the House): Correct. 
CHAMBER, LOBBIES, AND GALLERIES 
Customs Training Programme—Graduates 
Hon MAURICE WILLIAMSON (Minister of Customs) : I draw to the House’s 
attention that in the gallery today we have a stunning group of fine New Zealanders who 
are graduating from the customs training programme and becoming customs officers. 
QUESTIONS FOR ORAL ANSWER 
QUESTIONS TO MINISTERS 
Earthquake, Christchurch—Government Support for People Affected 
1. Hon ANNETTE KING (Deputy Leader—Labour) to the Prime Minister: Is he 
satisfied that all systems set up pursuant to commitments he has given to assist residents 
following the Christchurch earthquake are appropriate and working? 
Hon BILL ENGLISH (Deputy Prime Minister) on behalf of the Prime Minister: 
Generally yes, but due to severe damage in the eastern suburbs some households may 
well be without power, water, and sewerage for some time yet. However, I want to 
assure people that everythi ng that can be done is bein g done to restore essential 
infrastructure. 
Hon Annette King : Will he ask the Minister of Finance to issue a direction under 
section 12 of the Earthquake Commission Act requiring prompt and direct payment for 
rebuilding in Christchurch, in light of comments by the master plumbers’ chairman, 
Mark Whitehead, and builder Nick Rogers, who said today that they are refusing to 
carry out rebuilding work for the Earthquake Commission because they do not get paid, 
and they are now requiring distressed homeowners to pay cash up front before any work 
is done? 
Hon BILL ENGLISH: I do not think that the Earthquake Commission would need a 
direction to ensure that it does as much as it can do to expedite the rebuilding process. I 
understand the pressure particularly on contractors who were expecting the rebuild from 
the first earthquake to be well under way now. That has been delayed by maybe a month 
or two. But we will work with the commission to ensure it does it as fast as it can. 
Hon Annette King: In light of that answer, will th e Prime Minister ask the Minister 
of Finance to take urgent steps to ensure  contractors and subcontractors who are owed 
thousands of dollars by the Earthquake Commission for emergency work done after the 
September quake are paid, given that in orde r to avoid their businesses failing, with the 
loss of hundreds of jobs, some businesses have already taken out loans to stay afloat? 
Hon BILL ENGLISH : Certainly, if there are contractors who have not been paid, 
and who should have been paid according to normal credit terms, then the Earthquake 
17118 Questions for Oral Answer 10 Mar 2011 
Commission should get on and do that. But I think the signif icant shorter-term problem 
concerning the construction indus try in Christchurch was its expectation that it would 
be gearing up quite rapidly now, and that has been delayed by the second earthquake. 
All the parties involved, though, now have a gr eat deal more experience in how to get 
this work under way faster, and I hope it will be under way faster than last time round. 
Hon Annette King : Does he agree with Mayor Bob Parker that landlords who are 
hiking up rents on houses and business premises in Christchurch are “looting by another 
name”, and has he considered taking action similar to that of the Federal Government of 
the United States following Hurricane Katrina, when it limited the increase in rents, etc. 
to no more than 10 percent to prevent greedy landlords from profiting from other 
people’s misery? 
Hon BILL ENGLISH : We would share the mayor’s c oncern if there is significant 
profiteering. The Government will be liste ning to the advice of the Minister for 
Canterbury Earthquake Recovery, who is on the ground and also shares those concerns. 
Hon Annette King : Who is collating and acting on information about vulnerable 
residents—for example, elderly people who are living alone, people who are bedridden, 
and those with disabilities—when some ha ve been visited several times by various 
agencies, including M āori wardens, the police, the army, social agencies, etc., and 
others have not been visited at all, and how can the Government ensure that these 
people get the assistance they need? 
Hon BILL ENGLISH: As the member has pointed out, a number of agencies regard

Hon KATE WILKINSON (Minister of Labour) : I move, That the Canterbury 
Earthquake Commemoration Day Bill be now read a first time . I thank the House for 
supporting the passage of this bill through all its stages today. 
The bill provides for 18 March 2011 to be a day of commemoration in those parts of 
Canterbury—that is, in northern and central  Canterbury—that obs erve Christchurch 
Show Day as Canterbury Anniversary Day, in order to commemorate the devastating 
consequences of the Canterbury earthquake on 22 February 2011 at 12.51 p.m. Just over 
2 weeks have passed since Christchurch wa s shattered by its second major earthquake. 
This bill has been introduced to allow for the people of Canterbury to take a day to 
come together as a community, and as a regi on, to grieve together and mark an event 
that has so deeply affected each and every one of us. We are sti ll in the response stage 
10 Mar 2011 Canterbury Earthquake Commemoration Day Bill 17131 
of the earthquake. There is an enormous amou nt of work left to do, and that will be 
ongoing for years, but next Friday we want to take the time to provide an opportunity 
for all of Canterbury to mourn. It will also be a chance to celebrate the lives of those 
who have been lost. There is no denying that the wounds are still open for everyone to 
see. Next Friday’s memorial service will not bring an end to the grieving process, but I 
hope it will help Canterbury at the beginning of this long road ahead. 
This bill provides for next Friday to be observed as a public holiday known as 
Canterbury Earthquake Commemoration Day. Canterbury Earthquake Commemoration

Canterbury Anniversary Day, as  a one-off public holiday for the purposes of the 
Holidays Act 2003, and as a day to which s ection 65C(1) of the Education Act 1989 
applies, which requires schools to be closed.

public holidays will apply to Canterbury Earthquake Commemoration Day as follows: 
employees are entitled to be paid if Canterbury Earthquake Commemoration Day, 18 
March 2011, would have been a normal working day for them. If employees do not 
work on Canterbury Earthquake Commemoration Da y, they are entitled to be paid what 
they would have earned had they worked on the day; if employ ees work on the day, 
they should be paid at least time and a half  for the time they actually work on that day. 
They are also entitled to an  alternative holiday if the day would have been a normal 
working day for them. 
I am aware that this will place some unexp ected costs on some businesses in the 
region, and of course this was taken into c onsideration when the Government discussed 
creating a one-off public holiday for the regi on. However, there was no getting away 
from the fact that this eart hquake is the greatest tragedy ev er to strike the Canterbury 
region. Most people in Canterbury will want to attend the memorial service, but without 
a public holiday it would be much more difficult for many of them to do so. It is 
important that all of Canterbury is able to ta ke a day to mark this tragedy, and we hope

able to operate right now, and the Government is providing support to them and to 
thousands of employees.

that tens of thousands of people will want  to attend the memorial service, and I

people of northern and central Canterbury. I commend this bill to the House.

It is appropriate that we have a more fo rmal opportunity as a nation to mourn what

the opportunity to properly grieve with their loved ones. However, I think this memorial

mainly in the CTV building. They will all get to see that the whole of the New Zealand 
community is behind them and with them in their grief.  
I hope that the ceremony, to be held a week tomorrow, is more down-to-earth than 
many of the ceremonies that we as parliament arians are involved in. An image in my 
mind is of a whole lot of dignitaries in suits , ties, and for mal regalia, and that clashes 
with another image that is in my mind fr om the time I spent goi ng door-to-door in the 
suburb of Aranui, of people who have not been able to wash their clothes for more than

2 weeks, whose toilet is a bucket, and who will find it quite difficult to travel over the

It is unfortunate that ha ving a public ceremony so soon and declaring a public 
holiday has provoked quite a bit of angst a nd controversy amongst the good citizens of

buildings to reconstruct, or whether to continue with the Rugby World Cup at AMI

Although this memorial service is dedicate d to remembering those who died in the 
earthquake, it will inevitably be to some de gree an opportunity to express our feelings 
towards all those in Christchurch who have  suffered, and who are still suffering, as a 
result of the earthquake. Just about everyone living in the ea stern half of Christchurch 
has suffered some degree of trauma, and their nightmare has not  ended. Nerves are 
frayed from not knowing just how big the next aftershock will be, how much extra 
damage it might cause, and whether they will be hurt. Then there is the sadness at the 
loss of precious items in the big quake, wo rries about when homes will be repaired—if 
they can be—and where the money might come from. Add to that the daily grind for the 
many who are living without water and sewerage for the indefinite future. The memorial 
day will be an opportunity to remember those whose lives were lost, but we will also be 
thinking of those whose lives are now badl y damaged and who are living in their own 
version of hell.  
However, the story of Christchurch is also the story of great resilience, of community

[Greetings, Mr Assistant Speaker, and the H ouse, and to those listening in today to 
this broadcast. This is my first opportunity to offer up  words and farewells as others 
have done in these weeks past. This is my  first opportunity to stand here and say to

Coast mere months ago, your voices hereafte r mute. Depart to grea t Hawaiki, to long 
Hawaiki, to distant Hawaiki. Rest in the wo rld of the spirits who are to care and tend 
you. Returning here, to us, as we sit here—the remnants, so to speak—I greet us all.  
The disaster that fell on 22 February has for ever left an indelible mark on the hearts 
and the souls of the people of Aotearoa. Its ef fect was similar to the mining disaster on 
the West Coast. Some of the members of this House have visited Christchurch. You 
heard the lamentations. You sensed the pai n. You felt the foreboding of death. You saw 
the effects of the disaster and the pain borne by the individuals of  the region. I myself 
have not yet gone there. Perhaps I am fear ful of going, lest I see the collapsed 
buildings, lest I witness the rescue workers digging throug h the rubble, searching for 
bodies, and lament.  
Having to look upon those sights, I have no doubt that that is what would happen. 
Buildings can be rebuilt, students can in time return to school, and household 
possessions can eventually be replaced. I maintain, however, that the people of 
Christchurch will never see their dreams  realised, and pain, darkness, worry, and 
anxiety will be a permanent companion. For this, I extend my love.  
Allow me to turn to aspects of my M āori World, Mr Assistant Speaker, and speak of 
things therein that here pertain. One of those aspects or customs is at the heart of this 
bill. That custom is poroporoaki. What is poroporoaki? Poroporoaki is the opportunity 
given for the multitude, or individuals, usually at a marae, to speak to the departed. It 
matters not whether one person is lying in state, or two, or many deaths due to disaster. 
In a poroporoaki, words of fa rewell are offered to the deceased. There are times when 
harsh words may be uttered, but most speeches extol the virtues of the deceased, the 
good that people saw and heard. Often an opport unity is given for young people to say 
farewell, perhaps share things they never said to the person when he or she was alive.  
This is a time for acknowledging loss and expressing our grief. For it is the shedding 
of tears and mucus referred to by the Hon Pita  Sharples that alleviates some of the pain 
caused by death. Come the 18th day of this month, we will grieve; the whole country will 
be in mourning. So my question is, how c an the nation appropriate ly acknowledge and 
be engaged in the farewell to the dead? Fo r as the Hon Trevor Mallard only recently 
stated, there are difficulties. The Hon A nnette King and Keith Locke have also raised 
concerns. How do we pay our respects to them? How do we pay our respects to Joseph 
Pōhio of Christchurch? During the earthquake he dragged a woman away from danger. 
When his body was found it was taken to his marae to be mourned, then interred in the 
bosom of the earth. I understand he had worked for civil de fence for 21 years. How can 
we mourn this one if it has already been done?  
 And what of the parents of baby Tan eysha? She was only 5 weeks old. What about 
Baxter? He was only 5 months old. Those were babies who never got the chance to 
enjoy life. So many families are bereft, left without the wisdom and cultural heritage of 
their elders—Stuart and Lucy Routledge, childhood sweethearts, married for over 50 
years; grandmother Maureen Fletcher, ever remembered for her uplifting spirit—so 
many names and memories and shattered dreams that we in this House cannot possibly 
do justice to.  
I want to acknowledge the media for trying to record the stories of the dead. They 
told us about Jaime Gilbert, w ho died with a smile on his fa ce, knowing that his sister 
was out of harm’s way. They have accurately recorded this tragedy so that the people of 
the country and the world can know the calamity that has befallen Aotearoa.

JO GOODHEW (National—Rangitata): As I rise to sp eak on the Canterbury 
Earthquake Commemoration Day Bill, I need to  record my heartfelt sympathy to those 
who have suffered great loss as a result of the 22 February earthquake. Loss has come in 
many forms: loss of loved ones—and with that, loss of future dreams and plans—loss of 
homes and possessions, loss of businesses and jobs, and loss of what we knew to be the 
Christchurch we lived in, worked in, and visited. Here I must add an acknowledgment 
to those from overseas who are also mourning lost ones, and for some of them lost jobs, 
as well.  
This tragedy became international from the moment it happened. Reports of the 
earthquake sped rapidly around the world, and within minutes we were receiving texts 
and emails from people asking whether we we re OK. Some of those texts and emails 
were never received, and no reply with good news will ever be received, either. In a 
modern world with communication tools ap lenty, being out of communication causes 
immeasurable anxiety, particularly at a tim e like this. After the earthquake, cellphones 
helped to save lives, they helped to bring aid to those in need, and they brought good 
news to m
any, as well. We all looked at t hose texts with relief in  our hearts. But the 
silence of cellphones when answers were sought was unnerving and worrying, and in 
the end hinted at sorrow and loss.  
10 Mar 2011 Canterbury Earthquake Commemoration Day Bill 17141 
Although there has been great loss, co rrespondingly, great courage has been 
displayed and tremendous generosity exhibite d. Again, the internatio nal nature of this 
event has marked its gravity. Incredibly ra pidly, nations from ar ound the world offered 
their assistance, and New Zealand, as a nati on, said “Thank you. Yes, we do need your 
help.” We are a generous nation when it come s to offering our expertise to others in 
strife, so it was no great surprise that it was reciprocated. It was no surprise; 
nevertheless, it was a huge comfort to know that the numbers of our incredibly skilled 
emergency personnel and our urban search an d rescue people were to be massively 
swelled by ranks of Aussies, Singaporeans, Brits, Americans, Taiwanese, Chinese, and 
Japanese. We welcomed them with open arms.  
Emergency services people in fluoro vests and in uniform brought enormous comfort 
to a nation on edge, as we hoped against hope that more lives could be saved in the 
aftermath of the earthquake. The courage of those who have  been searching will spawn 
heart-warming and emotional stor ies that will become part of this nation’s history. The 
early searchers were actually the people w ho were caught up in the earthquake. They 
displayed sometimes superhuman efforts as they freed trapped people. We heard of

Hon KATE WILKINSON (Minister of Labour) : I move, That the Canterbury

contributions of other speakers so far. I think there is a wonderful opportunity for 
Canterbury to rebuild. After hearing the contribution from some of the Wellington 
speakers, I have to say that  if the Crusaders get too good the Hurricanes might not be 
able to beat them in the near future, but we certainly appreciate the gesture. I also 
appreciate that there was mutual agreement that the game that was due to be played be a 
draw.  
On a more serious note, this bill provide s for Friday, 18 March to be the day of 
commemoration to mark the tragedy that we have all suffered and the devastating 
consequences that it has brought. The death to ll of this day is yet to be officially 
confirmed, but we know that some 200 families may have lost a loved one. Those of us 
from Canterbury all have a link to someone who has died, whether it is a personal 
friend, a colleague, or a passi ng acquaintance whom we happened to meet. In some 
respects, though, the entire nation is grieving. Th e grief is, of course, most real for the 
people of Canterbury, but, none the less, I be lieve that the entire nation is grieving, and 
I certainly thank people for that.  
Tens of thousands of people have damaged homes and property. Many of those need 
to be rebuilt entirely. The entire region is exhausted by the continuing aftershocks. Our 
nerves are always on edge, and it is important that the region is provided with an 
opportunity to come together to grieve as a community. The memorial to take place next 
Friday will be a day of mour ning. It will be a difficult day for many of us, but I believe 
that it is crucial. I know that there are so me genuine concerns about the cost to some 
businesses, and this is the case for all public  holidays. But sometimes in the context of

allowing this day to be observed as a public ho liday is the best way to ensure that all 
Cantabrians have the opportunity  to attend the memorial at Ha gley Park, to take a step 
back from the carnage for a moment, and to grieve.

the support for Canterbury and for Christch urch during these tr agic times. I again 
commend the bill to the House.

generated so well amongst the people of Ch ristchurch, and, more broadly, across the

area of concern.

fix-up will take place—that is, people fixing up their houses. Of course, there is the 
whole question of replacing houses and which houses cannot be replaced. That is a very 
difficult problem for many people, but for people across the eastern part of Christchurch 
most buildings have some fix-up require d. Getting the insurance, getting the 
tradespeople—all of that stuff—will take a long time, and we have to be very supportive 
wherever we can. Parliament and the Government have to support creative solutions.

[Greetings, Mr Assistant Speaker. Mention has been made of the Māori World’s view 
on the Christchurch earthquake, so I will not ta ke that further. Let me begin by talking 
about a man from Waikato by the name of Tetaki Tair ākena. Recently he celebrated his 
60th birthday. To most, he was plain Wally.  To my knowledge, for over 25 years he 
taught the Māori language. He was very good at playing the guitar and was even in a 
band, according to some, alongside Steve Apira na. This Sunday he will lie in state on 
his marae at Tauwhare, close to  Morrinsville. He is one of  the ones who is about to be 
buried. So, yes, the most important thing is to acknow ledge those who are lost from 
sight. Death is something that cannot be avoided. 
 Is it a holiday that is ahead of us? I say it is not. A holiday is a time to rest and 
recuperate, to catch up on things that one is  not able to do on a wo rking day. Is this a 
17164 Canterbury Earthquake Commemoration Day Bill 10 Mar 2011 
holiday? No. It is a time to give thought to  those who have suffered the loss of loved 
ones, to offer help to those who are stil l grieving, and to grieve for those who have 
passed away. We must stand shoulder to shoulde r with the people over there, be it non-
Māori, Māori, people from beyond our shores, or migrants. That is the most important 
thing ahead of us. The principle cannot be faulted. Set aside a day for the people of that 
region of ours. I simply say that the Māori Party supports this emphatically.  
Personally, I believe that it is an opportunity  for us to acknowledge the rescue 
workers, the helpers, the ones who have worked tirelessly fo r that one of our 
communities, and indeed the nation—not just the ones from here in New Zealand, but 
those from overseas as well, particularl y the rescue workers from Japan, the police 
from Australia, and those all the way from th e United States of America, who came to 
support us.  
I particularly want to acknowledge all the voluntary organisations. It is most 
appropriate that we thank them immensely—M āori wardens of the country, the 
Salvation Army, the Rangiora Express, the Student Volunteer Army, the Farmy Army, 
the Red Cross, and the marae of the country. The marae opened up their doors to those 
with difficulties. Pipitea Marae just down the street along from us was one. It opened up 
its doors.  
But Ngāi Tahu must be accorded the greatest a ccolade. They were resolute in their 
efforts to lift morale and provide assistance and be a pillar and backbone for those who 
suffered hardship, whether they were non-M āori or Māori. They are currently set up at 
Wigram airbase. They have a telephone number to assist those seeking information and 
assistance relating to Pasifika people and other people. So a huge a ccolade is due to 
them and the financial help they provided fo r food and assistance. Ng āi Tahu have 
enormous foresight to help thos e living in the South Island. Ng ā Hau e Wh ā Marae is 
one that has opened up its doors to the Mi nistry of Social Development, which has 
become a recovery assistanc e centre. Thanks indeed to the Ministry of Mā ori 
Development and the non-governmental organisations.  
I acknowledge all the tribes of th e country that are part of me. M āori-medium 
schools have opened their door s to children within Ng āi Tahu to go and stay within me 
in Te Arawa.  
To conclude this address, I recall a huge disaster that oc curred in my area. It was 
the eruption of Tarawera in the year 1890. At that time, and according to the stories, 
150 of Ng āti Rangitihi-Tūhourangi perished. Te Arawa made clothing, land, and food 
available to the survivors, and that bond with Ng āti Wāhiao of W.hakarewarewa, Ngāti 
Hurunga of Ngāpuna, Tapuika of Waitangi, and Ngāti Rangitihi of Matatā still remains. 
The descend
ants are still there today, due to the great regard of these places within me 
in Te Arawa for those who suffered that huge earthquake. We have a similar situation 
again today, where the heart is opened up to assist and support those who have become 
victims of this disaster.  
I need to acknowledge Ng āti Porou; relatives of the Hon Hekia Parata; radio 
stations that raised money to help; M āori Television, for Hyundai CODE, releasing 
Glen Osborne and Reuben Wiki to sing, even if their efforts were not very flash; M āori-
medium schools and language nurseries of this locality, such as Te Kōhanga Reo o Ngā 
Mokopuna and Te K ōhanga Reo o Te Kaahui, which performed cultural items on 
Lambton Quay yesterday, as I was told; th e nurses from within me of Te Arawa; 
Waikato-Tainui, who sent their carpenters to  that place; and a person whom you may 
not know anything about, Mr Assistant Spea ker, Henare O’Keefe. This person is from 
Hastings. He owns a mobile barbecue kitchen. Its name is Tunutunu. He has taken it 
down there to barbecue food for the community.

Marae at Timaru—all have offered help. I extend my immense and heartfelt accolade, 
and that of the M āori Party and Parliament, as well,  to all those who supported the 
community here, which is grieving and hurting so strongly, in the hope that this day will 
be set aside. Celebrate those who have perish ed. Allow them to sleep and rest. The part

losses through death. Thank you to all of us, throughout the Chamber.]
